entries.7ededaf060f334efba7b38e400433cb5237df572: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv114"/><title type="x-ms">Second Corinthians</title> <div sID="gen31416" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">In</hi> his former epistle the apostle had signified his intentions of <hi type="italic">coming to Corinth, as he passed through Macedonia</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.5">xvi. 5</reference>), but, being providentially hindered for some time, he writes this second epistle to them about a year after the former; and there seem to be these two urgent occasions:—1. The case of the incestuous person, who lay under censure, required that with all speed he should be restored and received again into communion. This therefore he gives directions about (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.1-2Cor.2.17">ch. ii.</reference>), and afterwards (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1-2Cor.7.16">ch. vii.</reference>) he declares the satisfaction he had upon the intelligence he received of their good behaviour in that affair. 2. There was a contribution now making for the poor saints at Jerusalem, in which he exhorts the Corinthians to join, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1-2Cor.9.15">ch. viii., ix</reference>. <div eID="gen31417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31418" type="x-p"/> There are divers other things very observable in this epistle; for example, I. The account the apostle gives of his labours and success in preaching the gospel in several places, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.1-2Cor.2.17">ch. ii</reference>. II. The comparison he makes between the Old and New Testament dispensation, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1-2Cor.3.18">ch. iii</reference>. III. The manifold sufferings that he and his fellow-labourers met with, and the motives and encouragements for their diligence and patience, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1-2Cor.5.21">ch. iv., v</reference>. IV. The caution he gives the Corinthians against mingling with unbelievers, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1-2Cor.6.18">ch. vi</reference>. V. The way and manner in which he justifies himself and his apostleship from the opprobrious insinuations and accusations of false teachers, who endeavoured to ruin his reputation at Corinth, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.1-2Cor.12.21">ch. x.-xii.</reference>, and throughout the whole epistle. <div eID="gen31418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31419" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31420" type="x-p"/> After the introduction (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1-2Cor.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) the apostle begins with the narrative of his troubles and God's goodness, which he had met with in Asia, by way of thanksgiving to God (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.3-2Cor.1.6">ver. 3-6</reference>), and for the edification of the Corinthians, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.7-2Cor.1.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. Then he attests his and his fellow-labourers' integrity (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12-2Cor.1.14">ver. 12-14</reference>), and afterwards vindicates himself from the imputation of levity and inconstancy, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.24">ver. 15-24</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv114"/> <div eID="gen31420" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31419" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31421" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy <hi type="italic">our</hi> brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia: 2 Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to you and peace from God our Father, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen31421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31422" type="x-p"/> This is the introduction to this epistle, in which we have, <div eID="gen31422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31423" type="x-p"/> I. The inscription; and therein, 1. The person from whom it was sent, namely, Paul, who calls himself <hi type="italic">an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God.</hi> The apostleship itself was ordained by Jesus Christ, according to the will of God; and Paul was called to it by Jesus Christ, according to the will of God. He joins Timotheus with himself in writing this epistle; not because he needed his assistance, but that out of the mouth of two witnesses the word might be established; and this dignifying Timothy with the title of <hi type="italic">brother</hi> (either in the common faith, or in the work of the ministry) shows the humility of this great apostle, and his desire to recommend Timothy (though he was then a young man) to the esteem of the Corinthians, and give him a reputation among the churches. 2. The persons to whom this epistle was sent, namely, <hi type="italic">the church of God at Corinth:</hi> and not only to them, but also <hi type="italic">to all the saints in all Achaia,</hi> that is, to all the Christians who lived in the region round about. Note, In Christ Jesus no distinction is made between the inhabitants of city and country; all Achaia stands upon a level in his account. <div eID="gen31423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31424" type="x-p"/> II. The salutation or apostolical benediction, which is the same as in his former epistle; and therein the apostle desires the two great and comprehensive blessings, grace and peace, for those Corinthians. These two benefits are fitly joined together, because there is no good and lasting peace without true grace; and both of them come <hi type="italic">from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> who is the procurer and dispenser of those benefits to fallen man, and is prayed to as God.
entries.bdc42275a5767632749f6dd4b9f74685dee149d6: <div eID="gen31424" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Sufferings and Consolations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31425" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; <hi type="super">4</hi> Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God. <hi type="super">5</hi> For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ. <hi type="super">6</hi> And whether we be afflicted, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> for your consolation and salvation, which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer: or whether we be comforted, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> for your consolation and salvation. <div eID="gen31425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31426" type="x-p"/> After the foregoing preface, the apostle begins with the narrative of God's goodness to him and his fellow-labourers in their manifold tribulations, which he speaks of by way of thanksgiving to God, and to advance the divine glory (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.3-2Cor.1.6">v. 3-6</reference>); and it is fit that in all things, and in the first place, God be glorified. Observe, <div eID="gen31426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31427" type="x-p"/> I. The object of the apostle's thanksgiving, to whom he offers up blessing and praise, namely, the blessed God, who only is to be praised, whom he describes by several glorious and amiable titles. 1. <hi type="italic">The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ:</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho Theos kai pater tou Kyriou hemon Iesou Christou.</hi></hi> God is the Father of Christ's divine nature by eternal generation, of his human nature by miraculous conception in the womb of the virgin, and of Christ as God-man, and our Redeemer, by covenant-relation, and in and through him as Mediator our God and our Father, <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>. In the Old Testament we often meet with this title, <hi type="italic">The God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob,</hi> to denote God's covenant-relation to them and their seed; and in the New Testament God is styled <hi type="italic">the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> to denote his covenant-relation to the Mediator and his spiritual seed. <reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Gal. iii. 16</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">The Father of mercies.</hi> There is a multitude of tender mercies in God essentially, and all mercies are from God originally: mercy in his genuine offspring and his delight. <hi type="italic">He delighteth in mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mic. vii. 18</reference>. 3. <hi type="italic">The God of all comfort;</hi> from his proceedeth the <hi type="small-caps">Comforter</hi> , <reference osisRef="John.15.26">John xv. 26</reference>. He giveth the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.22">v. 22</reference>. All our comforts come from God, and our sweetest comforts are in him. <div eID="gen31427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31428" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons of the apostle's thanksgivings, which are these:— <div eID="gen31428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31429" type="x-p"/> 1. The benefits that he himself and his companions had received from God; for God <hi type="italic">had comforted</hi> them <hi type="italic">in all their tribulations,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4">v. 4</reference>. In the world they had trouble, but in Christ they had peace. The apostles met with many tribulations, but they found comfort in them all: their sufferings (which are called <hi type="italic">the sufferings of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">v. 5</reference>, because Christ sympathized with his members when suffering for his sake) did abound, but their consolation by Christ did abound also. Note, (1.) Then are we qualified to receive the comfort of God's mercies when we set ourselves to give him the glory of them. (2.) Then we speak best of God and his goodness when we speak from our own experience, and, in telling others, tell God also what he has done for our souls. <div eID="gen31429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31430" type="x-p"/> 2. The advantage which others might receive; for God intended that they <hi type="italic">should be able to comfort others</hi> in trouble (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4">v. 4</reference>), by communicating to them their experiences of the divine goodness and mercy; and the sufferings of good men have a tendency to this good end (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.6">v. 6</reference>) when they are endued with faith and patience. Note, (1.) What favours God bestows on us are intended not only to make us cheerful ourselves, but also that we may be useful to others. (2.) If we do imitate the faith and patience of good men in their afflictions, we may hope to partake of their consolations here and their salvation hereafter.
entries.f810274fe6d13c8737541187a6076cf356692834: <div eID="gen31430" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Sincerity and Affliction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31431" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And our hope of you <hi type="italic">is</hi> stedfast, knowing, that as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so <hi type="italic">shall ye be</hi> also of the consolation. <hi type="super">8</hi> For we would not, brethren, have you ignorant of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life: <hi type="super">9</hi> But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead: <hi type="super">10</hi> Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver <hi type="italic">us;</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift <hi type="italic">bestowed</hi> upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf. <div eID="gen31431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31432" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle speaks for the encouragement and edification of the Corinthians; and tells them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.7">v. 7</reference>) of his persuasion or stedfast hope that they should receive benefit by the troubles he and his companions in labour and travel had met with, that their faith should not be weakened, but their consolations increased. In order to this he tells them, 1. What their sufferings had been (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">We would not have you ignorant of our trouble.</hi> It was convenient for the churches to know what were the sufferings of their ministers. It is not certain what particular troubles in Asia are here referred to; whether the tumult raised by Demetrius at Ephesus, mentioned <reference osisRef="Acts.19.24-Acts.19.41">Acts xix.</reference>, or the fight with beasts at Ephesus, mentioned in the former epistle (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">ch. xv.</reference>), or some other trouble; for the apostle was in deaths often. This however is evident, that they were great tribulations. They <hi type="italic">were pushed out of measure,</hi> to a very extraordinary degree, above the common strength of men, or of ordinary Christians, to bear up under them, insomuch that they <hi type="italic">despaired even of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">v. 8</reference>), and thought they should have been killed, or have fainted away and expired. 2. What they did in their distress: <hi type="italic">They trusted in God.</hi> And they were brought to this extremity in order <hi type="italic">that they should not trust in themselves but in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, God often brings his people into great straits, that they may apprehend their own insufficiency to help themselves, and may be induced to place their trust and hope in his all-sufficiency. Our extremity is God's opportunity. <hi type="italic">In the mount will the Lord be seen;</hi> and we may safely trust in <hi type="italic">God, who raiseth the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">v. 9</reference>. God's raising the dead is a proof of his almighty power. He that can do this can do any thing, can do all things, and is worthy to be trusted in at all times. Abraham's faith fastened upon this instance of the divine power: <hi type="italic">He believed God who quickeneth the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Rom. iv. 17</reference>. If we should be brought so low as to despair even of life, yet we may then trust in God, who can bring back not only from the gates, but from the jaws, of death. 3. What the deliverance was that they had obtained; and this was seasonable and continued. Their hope and trust were not in vain, nor shall any who trust in him be ashamed. God had delivered them, and did still deliver them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.10">v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Having obtained help of God, they continued to that day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.22">Acts xxvi. 22</reference>. 4. What use they made of this deliverance: <hi type="italic">We trust that he will yet deliver us</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.10">v. 10</reference>), that God will deliver to the end, and <hi type="italic">preserve to his heavenly kingdom.</hi> Note, Past experiences are great encouragements to faith and hope, and they lay great obligations to trust in God for time to come. We reproach our experiences if we distrust God in future straits, who hath delivered as in former troubles. David, even when a young man, and when he had but a small stock of experiences, argued after the manner of the apostle here, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.37">1 Sam. xvii. 37</reference>. 5. What was desired of the Corinthians upon this account: <hi type="italic">That they would help together by prayer for them</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.11">v. 11</reference>), by social prayer, agreeing and joining together in prayer on their behalf. Note, our trusting in God must not supersede the use of any proper and appointed means; and prayer is one of those means. We should pray for ourselves and for one another. The apostle had himself a great interest in the throne of grace, yet he desires the help of others' prayers. If we thus help one another by our prayers, we may hope for an occasion of <hi type="italic">giving thanks by many</hi> for answer of prayer. And it is our duty not only to help one another with prayer, but in praise and thanksgiving, and thereby to make suitable returns for benefits received.
entries.9e2b4ab6e2a9168ca9fc9e43e2d88aab035a1e57: <div eID="gen31432" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Sincerity and Affliction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31433" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward. <hi type="super">13</hi> For we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge; and I trust ye shall acknowledge even to the end; 14 As also ye have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as ye also <hi type="italic">are</hi> ours in the day of the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen31433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31434" type="x-p"/> The apostle in these verses attests their integrity by the sincerity of their conversation. This he does not in a way of boasting and vain-glory, but as one good reason for desiring the help of prayer, as well as for the more comfortably trusting in God (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">Heb. xiii. 18</reference>), and for the necessary vindication of himself from the aspersions of some persons at Corinth, who reproached his person and questioned his apostleship. Here, <div eID="gen31434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31435" type="x-p"/> I. He appeals to the testimony of conscience with rejoicing (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">v. 12</reference>), in which observe, 1. The witness appealed to, namely, conscience, which is instead of a thousand witnesses. This God's deputy in the soul, and the voice of conscience is the voice of God. They rejoiced in the testimony of conscience, when their enemies reproached them, and were enraged against them. Note, The testimony of conscience for us, if that be right and upon good grounds, will be matter of rejoicing at all times and in all conditions. 2. The testimony this witness gave. And here take notice, Conscience witnessed, (1.) Concerning their conversation, their constant course and tenour of life: by that we may judge of ourselves, and not by this or that single act. (2.) Concerning the nature or manner of their conversation; that it was in simplicity and godly sincerity. This blessed apostle was a true Israelite, a man of plain dealing; you might know where to have him. He was not a man who seemed to be one thing and was another, but a man of sincerity. (3.) Concerning the principle they acted from in all their conversation, both in the world and towards these Corinthians; and that was not fleshly wisdom, nor carnal politics and worldly views, but it was the grace of God, a vital gracious principle in their hearts, that cometh from God, and tendeth to God. Then will our conversation be well ordered when we live and act under the influence and command of such a gracious principle in the heart. <div eID="gen31435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31436" type="x-p"/> II. He appeals to the knowledge of the Corinthians with hope and confidence, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.13-2Cor.1.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Their conversation did in part fall under the observation of the Corinthians; and these knew how they behaved themselves, <hi type="italic">how holily, and justly, and unblamably;</hi> they never found any thing in them unbecoming an honest man. This they had acknowledged in part already, and he doubted not but they would still do so to the end, that is, that they would never have any good reason to think or say otherwise of him, but that he was an honest man. And so there would be mutual rejoicing in one another. <hi type="italic">We are your rejoicing, even as you also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.</hi> Note, It is happy when ministers and people do rejoice in each other here; and this joy will be complete in that day when the great Shepherd of the sheep shall appear.
entries.d9d1dd3604eb43056b52542f07310b2dabffc8a9: <div eID="gen31436" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Sincerity and Affliction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31437" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And in this confidence I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit; <hi type="super">16</hi> And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judæa. <hi type="super">17</hi> When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay? <hi type="super">18</hi> But <hi type="italic">as</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> true, our word toward you was not yea and nay. <hi type="super">19</hi> For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, <hi type="italic">even</hi> by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. <hi type="super">20</hi> For all the promises of God in him <hi type="italic">are</hi> yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us. <hi type="super">21</hi> Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, <hi type="italic">is</hi> God; <hi type="super">22</hi> Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. 23 Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth. <hi type="super">24</hi> Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand. <div eID="gen31437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31438" type="x-p"/> The apostle here vindicates himself from the imputation of levity and inconstancy, in that he did not hold his purpose of coming to them at Corinth. His adversaries there sought all occasions to blemish his character, and reflect upon his conduct; and, it seemed, they took hold of this handle to reproach his person and discredit his ministry. Now, for his justification, <div eID="gen31438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31439" type="x-p"/> I. He avers the sincerity of his intention (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.17">v. 15-17</reference>), and he does this in confidence of their good opinion of him, and that they would believe him, when he assured them he <hi type="italic">was minded,</hi> or did really intend, <hi type="italic">to come</hi> to them, and that with the design, not that he might receive, but that they might receive a <hi type="italic">second benefit,</hi> that is, a further advantage by his ministry. He tells them that he had not herein <hi type="italic">used lightness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.17">v. 17</reference>), that, as he aimed not at any secular advantage to himself (for his purpose was not <hi type="italic">according to the flesh,</hi> that is, with carnal views and aims), so it was not a rash and inconsiderate resolution that he had taken up, for he had laid his measures thus of <hi type="italic">passing by them to Macedonia, and coming again to them from Macedonia in his way to Judea</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.16">v. 16</reference>), and therefore they might conclude that it was for some weighty reasons that he had altered his purpose; and that with him there was not yea yea, and nay nay, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.17">v. 17</reference>. He was not to be accused of levity and inconstancy, nor a contradiction between his words and intentions. Note, Good men should be careful to preserve the reputation of sincerity and constancy; they should not resolve but upon mature deliberation, and they will not change their resolves but for weighty reasons. <div eID="gen31439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31440" type="x-p"/> II. He would not have the Corinthians to infer that his gospel was false or uncertain, nor that it was contradictory in itself, nor unto truth, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.18-2Cor.1.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. For if it had been so, that he had been fickle in his purposes, or even false in the promises he made of coming to them (which he was not justly to be accused of, and so some understand his expression, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.18">v. 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">Our word towards you was not yea and nay</hi>), yet it would not follow that the gospel preached not only by him, but also by others in full agreement with him, was either false or doubtful. For <hi type="italic">God is true, and the Son of God, Jesus Christ,</hi> is true. The true God, and eternal life. Jesus Christ, whom the apostle preached, is not <hi type="italic">yea</hi> and <hi type="italic">nay,</hi> but in him was <hi type="italic">yea</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.19">v. 19</reference>), nothing but infallible truth. And the promises of God in Christ are not yea and nay, but yea and amen, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">v. 20</reference>. There is an inviolable constancy and unquestionable sincerity and certainty in all the parts of the gospel of Christ. If in the promises that the ministers of the gospel make as common men, and about their own affairs, they see cause sometimes to vary from them, yet the promises of the gospel covenant, which they preach, stand firm and inviolable. Bad men are false; good men are fickle; but <hi type="italic">God is true,</hi> neither fickle nor false. The apostle, having mentioned the stability of the divine promises, makes a digression to illustrate this great and sweet truth, that all the promises of God are yea and amen. For, 1. They are the promises of the God of truth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">v. 20</reference>), of him <hi type="italic">that cannot lie,</hi> whose truth as well as mercy endureth for ever. 2. They are made in Christ Jesus (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">v. 20</reference>), the Amen, the true and faithful witness; he hath purchased and ratified the covenant of promises, and is the <hi type="italic">surety of the covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.22">Heb. vii. 22</reference>. 3. They are confirmed by the Holy Spirit. He does establish Christians in the faith of the gospel; he has anointed them with his sanctifying grace, which in scripture is often compared to oil; he has sealed them, for their security and confirmation; and he is given <hi type="italic">as an earnest in their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.21-2Cor.1.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. An earnest secures the promise, and is part of the payment. The illumination of the Spirit is an earnest of everlasting life; and the comforts of the Spirit are an earnest of everlasting joy. Note, The veracity of God, the mediation of Christ, and the operation of the Spirit, are all engaged that the promises shall be sure to all the seed, and the accomplishment of them shall be to the <hi type="italic">glory of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">v. 20</reference>) for the glory of his rich and sovereign grace, and never-failing truth and faithfulness. <div eID="gen31440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31441" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle gives a good reason why he did not come to Corinth, as was expected, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.23">v. 23</reference>. It was that he might spare them. They ought therefore to own his kindness and tenderness. He knew there were things amiss among them, and such as deserved censure, but was desirous to show tenderness. He assures them that this is the true reason, after this very solemn manner: <hi type="italic">I call God for a record upon my soul</hi>—a way of speaking not justifiable where used in trivial matters; but this was very justifiable in the apostle, for his necessary vindication, and for the credit and usefulness of his ministry, which was struck at by his opposers. He adds, to prevent mistakes, that he did not pretend to have any dominion over their faith, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.24">v. 24</reference>. Christ only is the Lord of our faith; he is the <hi type="italic">author and finisher of our faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>. He reveals to us what we must believe. Paul, and Apollos, and the rest of the apostles, were <hi type="italic">but ministers by whom they believed</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">1 Cor. iii. 5</reference>), and so the <hi type="italic">helpers of their joy,</hi> even the joy of faith. For by faith we stand firmly, and live safely and comfortably. Our strength and ability are owing to faith, and our comfort and joy must flow from faith.  <chapter eID="2Cor.1"/> <div eID="gen31441" type="x-p"/>

entries.3f7592e98fed7d406e7efdc4b92fccfc4ea0b8c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17169"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen34044" type="x-p"/> The following reasons seem to have induced Paul to write this Second Epistle to the Corinthians: (1) That he might explain the reasons for his having deferred to pay them his promised visit, by taking Corinth as his way to Macedonia (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.19">1Co 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15">2Co 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.5">1Co 16:5</reference>); and so that he might set forth to them his apostolic walk in general (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Co 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.3-1Cor.6.13">6:3-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">7:2</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">2</reference>) That he might commend their obedience in reference to the directions in his First Epistle, and at the same time direct them now to forgive the offender, as having been punished sufficiently (2Co 2:1-11; 7:6-16). (3) That he might urge them to collect for the poor saints at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1-2Cor.9.15">2Co 8:1-9, 15</reference>). (4) That he might maintain his apostolic authority and reprove gainsayers.<div eID="gen34044" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34043" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34045" type="x-p"/> The external testimonies for its genuineness are Irenæus [Against Heresies, 3,7,1]; Athenagoras [Of the Resurrection of the Dead]; Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 3, p. 94; 4, p. 101]; Tertullian [On Modesty, 13].<div eID="gen34045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34046" type="x-p"/> The TIME OF WRITING was after Pentecost, A.D. 57, when Paul left Ephesus for Troas. Having stayed in the latter place for some time preaching the Gospel with effect (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>), he went on to Macedonia, being eager to meet Titus there, having been disappointed in his not coming to Troas, as had been agreed on between them. Having heard from him the tidings he so much desired of the good effect produced on the Corinthians by his First Epistle, and after having tested the liberality of the Macedonian churches (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">2Co 8:1</reference>), he wrote this Second Epistle, and then went on to Greece, where he abode for three months; and then, after travelling by land, reached Philippi on his return at Passover or Easter, A.D. 58 (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.1-Acts.20.6">Ac 20:1-6</reference>). So that this Epistle must have been written about autumn, A.D. 57.<div eID="gen34046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34047" type="x-p"/> Macedonia was THE PLACE from which it was written (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">2Co 9:2</reference>, where the present tense, "I boast," or "am boasting," implies his presence then in Macedonia). In Asia (Lydian Asia) he had undergone some great peril of his life (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">2Co 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>), whether the reference be [Paley] to the tumult at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.23-Acts.19.41">Ac 19:23-41</reference>), or, as Alford thinks, to a dangerous illness in which he despaired of life. Thence he passed by Troas to Philippi, the first city which would meet him in entering Macedonia. The importance of the Philippian Church would induce him to stay there some time; as also his desire to collect contributions from the Macedonian churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem. His anxiety of mind is recorded (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>) as occurring when he came into Macedonia, and therefore must have been at Philippi, which was the first city of Macedonia in coming from Troas; and here, too, from <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">2Co 7:6</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>, must have been the scene of his receiving the comforting tidings from Titus. "Macedonia" is used for Philippi in <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>, as is proved by comparison with <reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">16</reference>. So it is probably used here (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>). Alford argues from <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">2Co 8:1</reference>, where he speaks of the "grace bestowed on the churches (plural) of Macedonia," that Paul must have visited other churches in Macedonia, besides Philippi, when he wrote, for example, Thessalonica, Berea, &c., and that Philippi, the first on his route, is less likely to have been the scene of his writing than the last on his route, whichever it was, perhaps Thessalonica. But Philippi, as being the chief town of the province, was probably the place to which all the collections of the churches were sent. Ancient tradition, too (as appears from the subscription to this Epistle), favors the view that Philippi was the place from which this Epistle was sent by the hands of Titus who received, besides, a charge to prosecute at Corinth the collection which he had begun at his first visit (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>).<div eID="gen34047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34048" type="x-p"/> The STYLE is most varied, and passes rapidly from one phase of feeling to another; now joyous and consolatory, again severe and full of reproof; at one time gentle and affectionate, at another, sternly rebuking opponents and upholding his dignity as an apostle. This variety of style accords with the warm and earnest character of the apostle, which nowhere is manifested more beautifully than in this Epistle. His bodily frailty, and the chronic malady under which he suffered, and which is often alluded to (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Co 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.4">5:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.7-1Cor.12.9">12:7-9</reference>; compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">2Co 1:8</reference>), must have been especially trying to one of his ardent temperament. But besides this, was the more pressing anxiety of the "care of all the churches." At Corinth, as elsewhere, Judaizing emissaries wished to bind legal fetters of letter and form (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3-2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:3-18</reference>) on the freedom and catholicity of the Church. On the other hand, there were free thinkers who defended their immorality of practice by infidel theories (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.12">1Co 15:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32-1Cor.15.36">32-36</reference>). These were the "fightings without," and "fears within" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">6</reference>) which agitated the apostle's mind until Titus brought him comforting tidings from Corinth. Even then, while the majority at Corinth had testified their repentance, and, as Paul had desired, excommunicated the incestuous person, and contributed for the poor Christians of Judea, there was still a minority who, more contemptuously than ever, resisted the apostle. These accused him of crafty and mercenary motives, as if he had personal gain in view in the collection being made; and this, notwithstanding his scrupulous care to be above the possibility of reasonable suspicion, by having others besides himself to take charge of the money. This insinuation was palpably inconsistent with their other charge, that he could be no true apostle, as he did not claim maintenance from the churches which he founded. Another accusation they brought of cowardly weakness; that he was always threatening severe measures without daring to execute them (2Co 10:8-16; 13:2); and that he was vacillating in his teaching and practice, circumcising Timothy, and yet withholding circumcision from Titus; a Jew among the Jews, and a Greek among the Greeks. That most of these opponents were of the Judaizing party in the Church, appears from <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.22">2Co 11:22</reference>. They seem to have been headed by an emissary from Judea ("he that cometh," <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">2Co 11:4</reference>), who had brought "letters of commendation" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>) from members of the Church at Jerusalem, and who boasted of his purity of Hebrew descent, and his close connection with Christ Himself (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">23</reference>). His partisans contrasted his high pretensions with the timid humility of Paul (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.3">1Co 2:3</reference>); and his rhetoric with the apostle's plain and unadorned style (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.6">2Co 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.13">13</reference>). It was this state of things at Corinth, reported by Titus, that caused Paul to send him back forthwith thither with this Second Epistle, which is addressed, not to Corinth only (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1Co 1:2</reference>), but to all the churches also in Achaia (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>), which had in some degree been affected by the same causes as affected the Corinthian Church. The widely different tone in different parts of the Epistle is due to the diversity which existed at Corinth between the penitent majority and the refractory minority. The former he addresses with the warmest affection; the latter with menace and warning. Two deputies, chosen by the churches to take charge of the contribution to be collected at Corinth, accompanied Titus (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.18">2Co 8:18</reference>, 19, 22).<div eID="gen34048" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen34049" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1-2Cor.1.24">2Co 1:1-24</reference>. The Heading; Paul's Consolations in Recent Trials in Asia; His Sincerity towards the Corinthians; Explanation of His Not Having Visited Them as He Had Purposed.<div eID="gen34049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17169"/><hi type="bold">1. Timothy our brother--</hi>When writing to Timothy himself, he calls him "my son" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>). Writing of him, "brother," and "my beloved son" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:17</reference>). He had been sent before to Macedonia, and had met Paul at Philippi, when the apostle passed over from Troas to Macedonia (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1Co 16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen34050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all Achaia--</hi>comprising Hellas and the Peloponnese. The Gentiles themselves, and Annæus Gallio, the proconsul (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.12-Acts.18.16">Ac 18:12-16</reference>), strongly testified their disapproval of the accusation brought by the Jews against Paul. Hence, the apostle was enabled to labor in the whole province of Achaia with such success as to establish several churches there (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.8">1Th 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.4">2Th 1:4</reference>), where, writing from Corinth, he speaks of the "churches," namely, not only the Corinthian, but others also--Athens, Cenchrea, and, perhaps, Sicyon, Argos, &c. He addresses "the Church in Corinth," directly, and all "the saints" in the province, indirectly. In <reference osisRef="Gal.1.2">Ga 1:2</reference> all the "churches" are addressed directly in the same circular Epistle. Hence, here he does not say, all the churches, but "all the saints." <div eID="gen34051" type="x-p"/>
entries.c87e5eb2cc967d39b8e1ad11f567925efa4e76b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17170"/><div sID="gen34052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17170"/>3. This thanksgiving for his late deliverance forms a suitable introduction for conciliating their favorable reception of his reasons for not having fulfilled his promise of visiting them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.24">2Co 1:15-24</reference>).<div eID="gen34052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Father of mercies--</hi>that is, the SOURCE of all mercies (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen34053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comfort--</hi>which flows from His "mercies" experienced. Like a true man of faith, he mentions "mercies" and "comfort," before he proceeds to speak of afflictions (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4-2Cor.1.6">2Co 1:4-6</reference>). The "tribulation" of believers is not inconsistent with God's mercy, and does not beget in them suspicion of it; nay, in the end they feel that He is "the God of ALL comfort," that is, who imparts the only true and perfect comfort in every instance (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.3">Psa 146:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">5, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.11">Jas 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen34054" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc23e4a43fc4c34196691bf4ab1760fcfedfe47a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17171"/><div sID="gen34055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17171"/><hi type="bold">4. us--</hi>idiomatic for me (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.18">1Th 2:18</reference>).<div eID="gen34055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we may ... comfort them which are in any trouble--</hi>Translate, as the Greek is the same as before, "tribulation." The apostle lived, not to himself, but to the Church; so, whatever graces God conferred on him, he considered granted not for himself alone, but that he might have the greater ability to help others [Calvin]. So participation in all the afflictions of man peculiarly qualified Jesus to be man's comforter in all his various afflictions (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4-Isa.50.6">Is 50:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.15">He 4:15</reference>). <div eID="gen34056" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfc970b24f935f82d8dfa7607b924da03870c43a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17172"/><div sID="gen34057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17172"/><hi type="bold">5. sufferings--</hi>standing in contrast with "salvation" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.6">2Co 1:6</reference>); as "tribulation" (distress of mind), with comfort or "consolation."<div eID="gen34057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Christ--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>. The sufferings endured, whether by Himself, or by His Church, with which He considers Himself identified (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.40">Mt 25:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.45">45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.4">Ac 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.17-1John.4.21">1Jo 4:17-21</reference>). Christ calls His people's sufferings His own suffering: (1) because of the sympathy and mystical union between Him and us (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Ro 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">1Co 4:10</reference>); (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>) They are borne for His sake; (3) They tend to His glory (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen34058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abound in us--</hi>Greek, "abound unto us." The order of the Greek following words is more forcible than in English Version, "Even so through Christ aboundeth also our comfort." The sufferings (plural) are many; but the consolation (though singular) swallows up them all. Comfort preponderates in this Epistle above that in the first Epistle, as now by the effect of the latter most of the Corinthians had been much impressed. <div eID="gen34059" type="x-p"/>
entries.06580c2345075f9908138b00ef950d5290f096e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17173"/><div sID="gen34060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17173"/><hi type="bold">6. we ... afflicted ... for your consolation--</hi>exemplifying the communion of saints. Their hearts were, so to speak, mirrors reflecting the likenesses of each other (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.26">Php 2:26</reference>, 27) [Bengel]. Alike the afflictions and the consolations of the apostle tend, as in him so in them, as having communion with him, to their consolation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4">2Co 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">4:15</reference>). The Greek for "afflicted" is the same as before, and ought to be translated, "Whether we be in tribulation."<div eID="gen34060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is effectual--</hi>literally, "worketh effectually."<div eID="gen34061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the enduring, &c.--</hi>that is, in enabling you to endure "the same sufferings which we also suffer." Here follows, in the oldest manuscripts (not as English Version in the beginning of <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.7">2Co 1:7</reference>), the clause, "And our hope is steadfast on your behalf." <div eID="gen34062" type="x-p"/>
entries.e453275b9e4037b9f51567aaa5584a77bd0723f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17174"/><div sID="gen34063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17174"/><hi type="bold">7. so shall ye be--</hi>rather, "So are ye." He means, there is a community of consolation, as of suffering, between me and you. <div eID="gen34063" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fd2cc69975c40fa48faf1d840d5aa8f24601a06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17175"/><div sID="gen34064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17175"/>8-9. Referring to the imminent risk of life which he ran in Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.23-Acts.19.41">Ac 19:23-41</reference>) when the whole multitude were wrought up to fury by Demetrius, on the plea of Paul and his associates having assailed the religion of Diana of Ephesus. The words (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">2Co 1:9</reference>), "we had the sentence of death in ourselves," mean, that he looked upon himself as a man condemned to die [Paley]. Alford thinks the danger at Ephesus was comparatively so slight that it cannot be supposed to be the subject of reference here, without exposing the apostle to a charge of cowardice, very unlike his fearless character; hence, he supposes Paul refers to some deadly sickness which he had suffered under (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">2Co 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>). But there is little doubt that, had Paul been found by the mob in the excitement, he would have been torn in pieces; and probably, besides what Luke in Acts records, there were other dangers of an equally distressing kind, such as, "lyings in wait of the Jews" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.19">Ac 20:19</reference>), his ceaseless foes. They, doubtless, had incited the multitude at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.9">Ac 19:9</reference>), and were the chief of the "many adversaries" and "[wild] beasts," which he had to fight with there (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">16:9</reference>). His weak state of health at the time combined with all this to make him regard himself as all but dead (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.29">2Co 11:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">12:10</reference>). What makes my supposition probable is, that the very cause of his not having visited Corinth directly as he had intended, and for which he proceeds to apologize (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.23">2Co 1:15-23</reference>), was, that there might be time to see whether the evils arising there not only from Greek, but from Jewish disturbers of the Church (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.29">2Co 11:29</reference>), would be checked by his first Epistle; there not being fully so was what entailed on him the need of writing this second Epistle. His not specifying this here expressly is just what we might expect in the outset of this letter; towards the close, when he had won their favorable hearing by a kindly and firm tone, he gives a more distinct reference to Jewish agitators (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.22">2Co 11:22</reference>).<div eID="gen34064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">above strength--</hi>that is, ordinary, natural powers of endurance.<div eID="gen34065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despaired--</hi>as far as human help or hope from man was concerned. But in respect to help from God we were "not in despair" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8">2Co 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen34066" type="x-p"/>
entries.aef7480be683898ccd5cf05bf28e536131ef37a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17177"/><div sID="gen34069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17177"/><hi type="bold">10. doth deliver--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "will deliver," namely, as regards immediately imminent dangers. "In whom we trust that He will also (so the Greek) yet deliver us," refers to the continuance of God's delivering help hereafter. <div eID="gen34069" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4299655a8437dd8b0b0e54f835f1554be41523c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17178"/><div sID="gen34070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17178"/><hi type="bold">11. helping together by prayer for us--</hi>rather, "helping together on our behalf by your supplication"; the words "for us" in the Greek following "helping together," not "prayer."<div eID="gen34070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that for the gift, &c.--</hi>literally, "That on the part of many persons the gift (literally, 'gift of grace'; the mercy) bestowed upon us by means of (that is, through the prayers of) many may be offered thanks for (may have thanks offered for it) on our behalf." <div eID="gen34071" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cfd519e23ae633ed2907c438e4ec635172c7244: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17179"/><div sID="gen34072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17179"/><hi type="bold">12. For--</hi>reason why he may confidently look for their prayers for him.<div eID="gen34072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our rejoicing--</hi>Greek, "our glorying." Not that he glories in the testimony of his conscience, as something to boast of; nay, this testimony is itself the thing in which his glorying consists.<div eID="gen34073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in simplicity--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts read, "in holiness." English Version reading is perhaps a gloss from <reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference> [Alford]. Some of the oldest manuscripts and versions, however, support it.<div eID="gen34074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">godly sincerity--</hi>literally, "sincerity of God"; that is, sincerity as in the presence of God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.8">1Co 5:8</reference>). We glory in this in spite of all our adversities. Sincerity in Greek implies the non-admixture of any foreign element. He had no sinister or selfish aims (as some insinuated) in failing to visit them as he had promised: such aims belonged to his adversaries, not to him (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>). "Fleshly wisdom" suggests tortuous and insincere courses; but the "grace of God," which influenced him by God's gifts (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.3">Ro 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.15">15:15</reference>), suggests holy straightforwardness and sincere faithfulness to promises (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.17-2Cor.1.20">2Co 1:17-20</reference>), even as God is faithful to His promises. The prudence which subserves selfish interests, or employs unchristian means, or relies on human means more than on the Divine Spirit, is "fleshly wisdom."<div eID="gen34075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the world--</hi>even in relation to the world at large, which is full of disingenuousness.<div eID="gen34076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">more abundantly to you-ward--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">2Co 2:4</reference>). His greater love to them would lead him to manifest, especially to them, proofs of his sincerity, which his less close connection with the world did not admit of his exhibiting towards it. <div eID="gen34077" type="x-p"/>
entries.9faa847443b80f7fde2ac77645161ef620304891: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17180"/><div sID="gen34078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17180"/>13. We write none other things (in this Epistle) than what ye read (in my former Epistle [Bengel]; present, because the Epistle continued still to be read in the Church as an apostolic rule). Conybeare and Howson think Paul had been suspected of writing privately to some individuals in the Church in a different strain from that of his public letters; and translates, "I write nothing else to you but what ye read openly (the Greek meaning, 'ye read aloud,' namely, when Paul's Epistles were publicly read in the congregation, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.27">1Th 5:27</reference>); yea, and what you acknowledge inwardly."<div eID="gen34078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or acknowledge--</hi>Greek, "or even acknowledge." The Greek for "read" and for "acknowledge" are words kindred in sound and root. I would translate, "None other things than what ye know by reading (by comparing my former Epistle with my present Epistle), or even know as a matter of fact (namely, the consistency of my acts with my words)."<div eID="gen34079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even to the end--</hi>of my life. Not excluding reference to the day of the Lord (end of <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.14">2Co 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>). <div eID="gen34080" type="x-p"/>
entries.de07a7a187f40ea63b8dbcf800683d3221452333: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17181"/><div sID="gen34081" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17181"/><hi type="bold">14. in part--</hi>In contrast to "even to the end": the testimony of his life was not yet completed [Theophylact and Bengel]. Rather, "in part," that is, some of you, not all [Grotius, Alford]. So in <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">2Co 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference>. The majority at Corinth had shown a willing compliance with Paul's directions in the first Epistle: but some were still refractory. Hence arises the difference of tone in different parts of this Epistle. See Introduction.<div eID="gen34081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your rejoicing--</hi>your subject of glorying or boast. "Are" (not merely shall be) implies the present recognition of one another as a subject of mutual glorying: that glorying being about to be realized in its fulness "in the day (of the coming) of the Lord Jesus." <div eID="gen34082" type="x-p"/>
entries.36043661bc554222900ad332d98da4ccdb861954: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17182"/><div sID="gen34083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17182"/><hi type="bold">15. in this confidence--</hi>of my character for sincerity being "acknowledged" by you (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12-2Cor.1.14">2Co 1:12-14</reference>).<div eID="gen34083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was minded--</hi>I was intending.<div eID="gen34084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before--</hi>"to come unto you before" visiting Macedonia (where he now was). Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.5">1Co 16:5</reference>; also see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.18">1Co 4:18</reference>, which, combined with the words here, implies that the insinuation of some at Corinth, that he would not come at all, rested on the fact of his having thus disappointed them. His change of intention, and ultimate resolution of going through Macedonia first, took place before his sending Timothy from Ephesus into Macedonia, and therefore (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:17</reference>) before his writing the first Epistle. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.19.21">Ac 19:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">22</reference> (the order there is "Macedonia and Achaia," not Achaia, Macedonia); <reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">Ac 20:1</reference>, 2.<div eID="gen34085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye might have a second benefit--</hi>one in going to, the other in returning from, Macedonia. The "benefit" of his visits consisted in the grace and spiritual gifts which he was the means of imparting (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.11">Ro 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen34086" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac16262ee033fb2396e4e1aacc5c8d319ab2e213: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17183"/><div sID="gen34087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17183"/><hi type="bold">16. This intention of visiting them on the way to Macedonia, as well as after having passed through it, must have reached the ears of the Corinthians in some way or other--</hi>perhaps in the lost Epistle (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.18">1Co 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.9">5:9</reference>). The sense comes out more clearly in the Greek order, "By you to pass into Macedonia, and from Macedonia to come again unto you." <div eID="gen34087" type="x-p"/>
entries.2aba4ac3a4413e2887e1407701eda7beae54c13e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17184"/><div sID="gen34088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17184"/><hi type="bold">17. use lightness--</hi>Was I guilty of levity? namely, by promising more than I performed.<div eID="gen34088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or ... according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea, yea ... nay, nay?--</hi>The "or" expresses a different alternative: Did I act with levity, or (on the other hand) do I purpose what I purpose like worldly (fleshly) men, so that my "yea" must at all costs be yea, and my "nay" nay [Bengel, Winer, Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.7">Mt 14:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.14.9">9</reference>)? The repetition of the "yea" and "nay" hardly agrees with Alford's view, "What I purpose do I purpose according to the changeable purposes of the fleshly (worldly) man, that there may be with me the yea yea, and the nay nay (that is, both affirmation and negation concerning the same thing)?" The repetition will thus stand for the single yea and nay, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.5.37">Mt 5:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.12">Jas 5:12</reference>. But the latter passage implies that the double "yea" here is not equivalent to the single "yea": Bengel's view, therefore, seems preferable. <div eID="gen34089" type="x-p"/>
entries.e19739a4c6e12a9b2741f7243ea52da7a3a7feb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17185"/><div sID="gen34090" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17185"/>18. He adds this lest they might think his DOCTRINE was changeable like his purposes (the change in which he admitted in <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.17">2Co 1:17</reference>, while denying that it was due to "lightness," and at the same time implying that not to have changed, where there was good reason, would have been to imitate the fleshly-minded who at all costs obstinately hold to their purpose).<div eID="gen34090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true--</hi>Greek, "faithful" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen34091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our word--</hi>the doctrine we preach.<div eID="gen34092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was not--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "is not."<div eID="gen34093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yea and nay--</hi>that is, inconsistent with itself. <div eID="gen34094" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2ebc5cb10b24b91aa8bcb00d445b32824f5a3f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17186"/><div sID="gen34095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17186"/>19. Proof of the unchangeableness of the doctrine from the unchangeableness of the subject of it, namely, Jesus Christ. He is called "the Son of God" to show the impossibility of change in One who is co-equal with God himself (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">1Sa 15:29</reference>; Mal 3:6).<div eID="gen34095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by me ... Silvanus and Timotheus--</hi>The Son of God, though preached by different preachers, was one and the same, unchangeable. Silvanus is contracted into Silas (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.22">Ac 15:22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.12">1Pe 5:12</reference>).<div eID="gen34096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in him was yea--</hi>Greek, "is made yea in Him"; that is, our preaching of the Son of God is confirmed as true in Him (that is, through Him; through the miracles wherewith He has confirmed our preaching) [Grotius]; or rather, by the witness of the Spirit which He has given (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.21">2Co 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>) and of which miracles were only one, and that a subordinate manifestation. <div eID="gen34097" type="x-p"/>
entries.c789a04b59799e54a3462d0875d44eee6a6608da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17187"/><div sID="gen34098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17187"/>20. Rather, How many soever be the promises of God, in Him is the "yea" ("faithfulness in His word": contrasted with the "yea and nay," <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.19">2Co 1:19</reference>, that is, inconstancy as to one's word).<div eID="gen34098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and in him Amen--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Wherefore through Him is the Amen"; that is, In Him is faithfulness ("yea") to His word, "wherefore through Him" is the immutable verification of it ("Amen"). As "yea" is His word, so "Amen" is His oath, which makes our assurance of the fulfilment doubly sure. Compare "two immutable things (namely, His word and His oath) in which it was impossible for God to lie" (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">He 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Re 3:14</reference>). The whole range of Old Testament and New Testament promises are secure in their fulfilment for us in Christ.<div eID="gen34099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the glory of God by us--</hi>Greek, "for glory unto God by us" (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">2Co 4:15</reference>), that is, by our ministerial labors; by us His promises, and His unchangeable faithfulness to them, are proclaimed. Conybeare takes the "Amen" to be the Amen at the close of thanksgiving: but then "by us" would have to mean what it cannot mean here, "by us and you." <div eID="gen34100" type="x-p"/>
entries.59b2126b9a4bb69e400df5a4b6d76f49c59834b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17188"/><div sID="gen34101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17188"/><hi type="bold">21. stablisheth us ... in Christ--</hi>that is, in the faith of Christ--in believing in Christ.<div eID="gen34101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anointed us--</hi>As "Christ" is the "Anointed" (which His name means), so "He hath anointed (Greek, "chrisas") us," ministers and believing people alike, with the Spirit (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.22">2Co 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>, 27). Hence we become "a sweet savor of Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2Co 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen34102" type="x-p"/>
entries.14e97cb087998aae6c14d3a376d3cbf814670f06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17189"/><div sID="gen34103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17189"/><hi type="bold">22. sealed--</hi>A seal is a token assuring the possession of property to one; "sealed" here answers to "stablisheth us" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.21">2Co 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.2">1Co 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen34103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the earnest of the Spirit--</hi>that is, the Spirit as the earnest (that is, money given by a purchaser as a pledge for the full payment of the sum promised). The Holy Spirit is given to the believer now as a first instalment to assure him his full inheritance as a son of God shall be his hereafter (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>). "Sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">Ro 8:23</reference>). The Spirit is the pledge of the fulfilment of "all the promises" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2Co 1:20</reference>). <div eID="gen34104" type="x-p"/>
entries.3821aee226e528ef759d5d5accef6a4191e4723e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17190"/><div sID="gen34105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17190"/><hi type="bold">23. Moreover I--</hi>Greek, "But I (for my part)," in contrast to God who hath assured us of His promises being hereafter fulfilled certainly (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20-2Cor.1.22">2Co 1:20-22</reference>).<div eID="gen34105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call God--</hi>the all-knowing One, who avenges wilful unfaithfulness to promises.<div eID="gen34106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a record upon my soul--</hi>As a witness as to the secret purposes of my soul, and a witness against it, if I lie (Mal 3:5).<div eID="gen34107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to spare you--</hi>in order not to come in a rebuking spirit, as I should have had to come to you, if I had come then.<div eID="gen34108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I came not as yet--</hi>Greek, "no longer"; that is, I gave up my purpose of then visiting Corinth. He wished to give them time for repentance, that he might not have to use severity towards them. Hence he sent Titus before him. Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.11">11</reference>, which shows that his detractors represented him as threatening what he had not courage to perform (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.18">1Co 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.19">19</reference>). <div eID="gen34109" type="x-p"/>
entries.9eaeb6ae27809f5e181c4a9ddfc65e8b98a99c90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17191"/><div sID="gen34110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17191"/><hi type="bold">24. Not for that--</hi>that is, Not that. "Faith" is here emphatic. He had "dominion" or a right to control them in matters of discipline, but in matters of "faith" he was only a "fellow helper of their joy" (namely, in believing, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.13">Ro 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.25">Php 1:25</reference>). The Greek is, "Not that we lord it over your faith." This he adds to soften the magisterial tone of <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.23">2Co 1:23</reference>. His desire is to cause them not sorrow (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.1">2Co 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>), but "joy." The Greek for "helpers" implies a mutual leaning, one on the other, like the mutually supporting buttresses of a sacred building. "By faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.20">Ro 11:20</reference>) ye stand"; therefore it is that I bestow such pains in "helping" your faith, which is the source of all true "joy" (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.13">Ro 15:13</reference>). I want nothing more, not to lord it over your faith. <chapter eID="2Cor.1"/>

entries.f1588b895ab8e5613200ffd9989a524a0bb0b2e9: <div eID="gen48703" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Second Epistle to the Corinthians</title> <div sID="gen48704" type="x-p"/> It is a general opinion among learned men that this epistle was written about a year after the former: and this seems to be supported by the words, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">2Cor 9:2</reference> : Achaia was ready a year ago; for the apostle having given instructions for that collection, to which he refers in these words at the close of the preceding epistle, they would not have had the forwardness there mentioned till a year had elapsed. As the apostle had purposed to stay at Ephesus till pentecost, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.8">1Cor 16:8</reference>; and he stayed some time in Asia after his purpose to leave Ephesus and go to Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.9.21">Act 9:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.9.22">Act 9:22</reference>; and yet making here his apology for not wintering in Corinth, as he thought to do, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.6">1Cor 16:6</reference>; this epistle must have been written after the winter, and consequently when a new year was begun. It therefore, says Dr. Whitby, seems to have been written after his second coming to Macedonia, mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.20.3">Act 20:3</reference>. For, (1.) It was written after he had been at Troas, and had left that place to return to Macedonia: now that was at his second going thither; see <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Cor 2:12</reference>. (2.) It was written when Timothy was with him: now, when he left Ephesus to go into Macedonia, Timothy went not with him, but was sent before him, <reference osisRef="Act.19.22">Act 19:22</reference>; but at his second going through Macedonia, Timothy was with him, <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>. (3.) He speaks of some Macedonians who were likely to accompany him, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">2Cor 9:4</reference>. Now, at his second going from Macedonia, there accompanied him Aristarchus, Secundus, and Gaius of Thessalonica, the metropolis of Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>. (4.) The postscript says that this epistle was written from Philippi, where Paul was till the days of unleavened bread, <reference osisRef="Act.20.6">Act 20:6</reference>; it therefore seems to have been sent from thence to them by Titus, and some other person, not long before St. Paul's coming to them; which he speaks of as instant, <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1">2Cor 13:1</reference>; and that which he was now ready to do, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2Cor 12:14</reference>; and did, according to Dr. Lightfoot, in his journey from Philippi to Troas; he sailing about from Philippi to Corinth, to make good his promise; whilst the rest that were with him, <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>, went directly the next cut to Troas, and there waited for him. See Whitby. <div eID="gen48704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48705" type="x-p"/> That the first epistle had produced powerful effects among the Corinthians is evident from what the apostle mentions in this. Titus had met him in Macedonia, and told him of the reformation produced by this epistle, see <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Cor 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">2Cor 7:6</reference>; that the Church had excommunicated the incestuous man; that the epistle had overwhelmed them with great distress; had led them to a close examination of their conduct and state; and had filled them with respect and affection for their apostle, etc. Hearing this, St. Paul wrote this second epistle, to comfort, to commend them, and to complete the work which he had begun, by causing them to finish the contribution for the poor saints at Jerusalem; and also to vindicate his own apostolic character, and to unmask the pretended apostle, who had led them so long astray. See the preceding Introduction. <div eID="gen48705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48706" type="x-p"/> Its principal divisions are: - <div eID="gen48706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48707" type="x-p"/> I. The preface, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1-2Cor.1.7">2Cor 1:1-7</reference>. <div eID="gen48707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48708" type="x-p"/> II. The Narration, comprehending an account of what had happened to himself; his answer to their questions concerning the incestuous person, with different other matters; among which, the following are the chief: - (1.) The persecution which he had suffered in Asia, and from which he had been miraculously rescued, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8-2Cor.1.14">2Cor 1:8-14</reference>. (2.) His purpose to pay them a visit, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.24">2Cor 1:15-24</reference>. (3.) Concerning the sorrow which they had suffered on account of the excommunication of the incestuous person, 2 Corinthians 2, 7. (4.) His own vindication against the false apostle; in which he gives an account of his doctrine, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6-2Cor.3.18">2Cor 3:6-18</reference>. His conduct, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1-2Cor.4.6">2Cor 4:1-6</reference>. His bodily infirmities, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Cor 4:7</reference>; and 2 Corinthians 5. (5.) Strongly exhorts them to a holy life, 2 Corinthians 6, 7. <div eID="gen48708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48709" type="x-p"/> III. Of the Alms that had been collected, and were yet to be collected, 2 Corinthians 8, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.1-2Cor.9.15">2Cor 9:1-15</reference>. <div eID="gen48709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48710" type="x-p"/> IV. His Defence against the false apostle and his calumniators in general, 2 Corinthians 10-12. <div eID="gen48710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48711" type="x-p"/> V. Miscellaneous matters, <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1-2Cor.13.14">2Cor 13:1-14</reference>. <div eID="gen48711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48712" type="x-p"/> It may be remarked, once for all, that none of these or such artificial divisions are made by the apostle himself, no more than the divisions into chapters and verses. All these are the work of man, and certainly contribute nothing to a proper understanding of the epistle itself. The apostle appears to have sat down, and, under the influence of the Divine Spirit, he wrote on the different subjects treated of in the epistle just in the order that these things occurred to his mind, without intending particular heads, divisions or subdivisions. And, as he probably wrote the whole with very little intermission of time, his sense will be best apprehended by those who carefully read over the whole at one sitting. <div eID="gen48712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48713" type="x-p"/> St. Paul encourages them to trust in God in all adversities, from a consideration of the support which he had granted them already in times of afflictions; and expresses his strong confidence of their fidelity, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1-2Cor.1.7">2Cor 1:1-7</reference>. Mentions the heavy tribulation which he had passed through in Asia; as also his deliverance, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8-2Cor.1.11">2Cor 1:8-11</reference>. Shows in what the exultation of a genuine Christian consists, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Cor 1:12</reference>. Appeals to their own knowledge of the truth of the things which he wrote to them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.13">2Cor 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.14">2Cor 1:14</reference>. Mentions his purpose of visiting them; and how sincere he was in forming it; and the reason why he did not come, as he had purposed, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.24">2Cor 1:15-24</reference>. <div eID="gen48713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48714" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen48714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48715" type="x-p"/> Paul, an apostle - Paul, commissioned immediately by Jesus Christ himself, according to the will of God, to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles. See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.1">1Cor 1:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen48715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48716" type="x-p"/> In all Achaia - The whole of the Peloponnesus, or that country separated from the main land by the Isthmus of Corinth. From this we may learn that this epistle was not only sent to the Church at Corinth, but to all the Churches in that country.
entries.f0d1b3cdd0f97a51e9563e6e6d54c567afc5af72: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen48716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48717" type="x-p"/> Grace be to you and peace - See <reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Rom 1:7</reference>.
entries.b64818501a43d308e934d9ab6ee06d6fd57cfa76: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen48717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48718" type="x-p"/> Blessed be God - Let God have universal and eternal praise: <div eID="gen48718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48719" type="x-p"/> 1. Because he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the gift of his endless love to man, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>. <div eID="gen48719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48720" type="x-p"/> 2. Because he is the Father of mercies, ὁ Πατηρ των οικτιρμων, the source whence all mercy flows, whether it respect the body or the soul, time or eternity; the source of tender mercy; for so the word implies. See on <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Rom 12:1</reference> (note). And, <div eID="gen48720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48721" type="x-p"/> 3. Because he is the God of all comfort - the Fountain whence all consolation, happiness, and bliss flow to angels and to men.
