As he saw that his afflictions were made by some an occasion of holding him in contempt, with the view of calling back the Corinthians from an error of this nature, <note n="231"> <div sID="gen120801" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Afin d’oster aux Corinthiens ceste mauuaise fantasie</foreign>;” — “With the view of ridding the Corinthians of this wicked fancy.”<div eID="gen120801" type="x-p"/> </note> he shows in the first place that he ought to be in high esteem among them, in consideration of advantage redounding to themselves; and then afterwards he associates them with himself, that they may reckon his afflictions to be in a manner their own. “Whether I suffer afflictions, or experience consolation, it is all for your benefit, and I cherish an assured hope, that you will continue to enjoy this advantage.” <note n="232"> <div sID="gen120802" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Iusques en la fin</foreign>;” — “Until the end.”<div eID="gen120802" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120803" type="x-p"/>For such were Paul’s afflictions, and his consolations also, that they would have contributed to the edification of the Corinthians, had not the Corinthians of their own accord deprived themselves of the advantage redounding from it. He, accordingly, declares his confidence in the Corinthians to be such, that he entertains the assured hope that it will not be vain, that he has been afflicted, and has received consolation for their advantage. The false apostles made every effort to turn to Paul’s reproach everything that befell him. Had they obtained their wish, the afflictions which he endured for their salvation, had been vain and fruitless; they would have derived no advantage from the consolations with which the Lord refreshed him. To contrivances of this nature he opposes his present confidence. His afflictions tended to promote the comfort of believers, as furnishing them with occasion of confirmation, on their perceiving that he suffered willingly, and endured with fortitude so many hardships for the sake of the gospel. For however we may acknowledge that afflictions ought to be endured by us for the sake of the gospel, we, nevertheless, tremble through a consciousness of our weakness, and think ourselves not prepared for it. <note n="233"> <div sID="gen120804" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et ne pensons point estre assez forts</foreign>;” — “And do not think that we are sufficiently strong.”<div eID="gen120804" type="x-p"/> </note> In that case, we should call to mind the examples of the saints, which should make us more courageous.<div eID="gen120803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120805" type="x-p"/>On the other hand, his personal consolation flowed out to the whole Church, inasmuch as they concluded, <note n="234"> <div sID="gen120806" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les fideles recueilloyent de là, et s’asseuroyent</foreign>;” — “Believers inferred from this, and assured themselves.”<div eID="gen120806" type="x-p"/> </note> that God who had sustained and refreshed him in his emergency, would, in like manner, not be wanting to them. Thus their welfare was promoted in both ways, and this is what he introduces as it were by way of parenthesis, when he says — <hi type="italic">which is made effectual in the endurance,</hi> etc. For he wished to add this clause, by way of explanation, that they might not think that they had nothing to do with the afflictions which he alone endured. Erasmus takes the participle <foreign xml:lang="el">γουμένης</foreign> in an active sense, <note n="235"> <div sID="gen120807" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Traduisant, Qui oeuure ou besongne</foreign>;” — “Rendering it, Which works or labors.”<div eID="gen120807" type="x-p"/> </note> but a passive signification is more suitable, <note n="236"> <div sID="gen120808" type="x-p"/> Dr. Bloomfield, in his Notes on <reference osisRef="Bible:1Thess.2.13">1 Thessalonians 2:13</reference>, explains <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐνεργεῖται</foreign>, to mean — “<hi type="italic">is made effectual</hi>,” or “shews itself in its effects,” and adds: “This view I find supported by the opinion of Schott, who maintains that <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐνεργεῖσθαι</foreign>, is never in the New Testament used as a <hi type="italic">middle</hi> form, with an active sense; but always (especially in St. Paul’s writings) as a <hi type="italic">passive</hi>. Indeed, Bp. Bull, Exam. p. 9, goes yet farther, and asserts, that it is scarcely ever so used, even in the <hi type="italic">Classical</hi> writers (I believe he might have said never) but always in a passive sense.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120808" type="x-p"/> </note> as Paul designed simply to explain in what respect everything that befell him was for their <hi type="italic">salvation. </hi>He says, accordingly, that he suffers, indeed, alone, but that his sufferings are of use for promoting their <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> — not as though they were expiations or sacrifices for sins, but as edifying them by confirming them. Hence he conjoins consolation and salvation, with the view of pointing out the way in which their salvation was to be accomplished.<div eID="gen120805" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120794" osisID="2Cor.1.6" type="section"/>
entries.090765f364bc459895ea287b8750e6bbbc9d50eb: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.7" sID="gen120809" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> <hi type="italic">Knowing, that as</hi> However there might be some of the Corinthians that were drawn away for the time by the calumnies of the false Apostles, so as to entertain less honorable views of Paul, on seeing him shamefully handled before the world, he, nevertheless, associates them with himself both in fellowship of afflictions, and in hope of consolation. <note n="237"> <div sID="gen120811" type="x-p"/> The Corinthians were <foreign xml:lang="el">κοινωνοί</foreign> <hi type="italic">partakers of</hi>, or <hi type="italic">in communion with him in his afflictions</hi>. What is more humble and lowly (<foreign xml:lang="el">τί ταπεινοφρωνέστερον</foreign>) than Paul in this expression? saith Chrysostom — they who had not in the least measure shared with him in sufferings, yet he maketh them copartners with him. They are, as Salmeron expresseth it, <hi type="italic">Copartners in the gain and in the loss with Paul</hi>. They venture (as it were) in the ship together.” — <hi type="italic">Burgesse</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120811" type="x-p"/> </note> Thus he corrects their perverse and malignant view, without subjecting them to an open rebuke.<div eID="gen120810" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120809" osisID="2Cor.1.7" type="section"/>
entries.0199956f7e24a3e394e792bca37912f847804ea6: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.8" sID="gen120812" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">For I would not have you ignorant</hi> He makes mention of the greatness and difficulty of his conflicts, that the glory of victory may thereby the more abundantly appear. Since the time of his sending them the former epistle, he had been exposed to great dangers, and had endured violent assaults. The probability, however, is that he refers here to the history, which Luke relates in <reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.23">Acts 19:23</reference>, though in that passage he does not so distinctly intimate the extent of the danger. As, however, he states that <hi type="italic">the whole city was in a tumult, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.29">Acts 19:29</reference>,) it is easy from this to infer the rest. For we know what is the usual effect of a popular tumult, when it has been once kindled. By this persecution Paul declares he had been oppressed <hi type="italic">beyond measure, </hi>nay more, <hi type="italic">above strength, </hi>that is, so as not to be able to endure the burden. For it is a metaphor taken from persons who give way under the pressure of a heavy load, or from ships that sink from being overladen — not that he had actually fainted, but that he felt that his strength would have failed him, if the Lord had not imparted fresh strength. <note n="238"> <div sID="gen120814" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Pressed above measure</hi>. (<foreign xml:lang="el">καθ ᾿ ὑπερβολὴν ἐβαρήςθημεν</foreign>.) The words <foreign xml:lang="el">βάρος</foreign> and <foreign xml:lang="el">βάρουμαι</foreign>, are applied sometimes to the enduring of a burden, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.20.12">Matthew 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.2">Galatians 6:2</reference>,) whether it be a temporal burden or spiritual [...] In this place it seemeth to be taken from porters, who have a burden imposed upon them, more than they are able to stand under; or as Chrysostom, from ships which are over much burdened, and so are in danger of being lost. And as if there were not emphasis enough in the word pressed, he addeth another to aggravate it — (<foreign xml:lang="el">καθ ᾿ ὑπερβολήν</foreign>) — <hi type="italic">above measure</hi> — <hi type="italic">Above strength</hi>. (<foreign xml:lang="el">ὑπὲρ δύναμιν</foreign>.) Chrysostom observeth this differeth from the other. For a burden may be exceeding heavy, yet to some mighty man it may not be above his strength. When <hi type="italic">Samson</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.3">Judges 16:3</reference>) carried away the gates of the city Gaza, with the posts and barre upon his shoulders, here was a burden out of measure heavy; no ordinary man could do so; but yet to <hi type="italic">Samson</hi> it was not above his strength. Thus it was with Paul, who may be called a <hi type="italic">spiritual Samson</hi>, for that heavenly might and power which God had endowed him with; he is assaulted with a trouble that was not only <hi type="italic">hyperbolically weighty</hi>, but also <hi type="italic">above his strength</hi>. Paul had no more power to stand under it.” — Burgesse on <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1">2 Corinthians 1</reference>, pp. 269, 270, 278. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120814" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120815" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">So that we were in anxiety even as to life itself</hi> — that is, “So that I thought life was gone, or at least I had very little hope of it remaining, as those are wont to feel who are shut up so as to see no way of escape.” Was then so valiant a soldier of Christ, so brave a wrestler, left without strength, so as to look for nothing but death? <note n="239"> <div sID="gen120816" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vn champion si preux et magnanime, perdoit — il courage attendant la mort</foreign>?” — “Did a champion so valiant and magnanimous lose heart, looking for nothing but death?”<div eID="gen120816" type="x-p"/> </note> For he mentions it as the reason of what he had stated — that he <hi type="italic">despaired of life. </hi>I have already observed, that Paul does not measure his strength in connection with help from God, but according to his own personal feeling of his ability. Now there can be no doubt, that all human strength must give way before the fear of death. Farther, it is necessary that even saints themselves should be in danger of an entire failure of strength, that, being put in mind of their own weakness, they may learn, agreeably to what follows, to place their entire dependence on God alone. At the same time I have preferred to explain the word <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐξαπορεῖσθαι</foreign>, which is made use of by Paul, as denoting a <hi type="italic">trembling anxiety, </hi>rather than render it, as Erasmus has done by the word <hi type="italic">despair; </hi>because he simply means, that he was hemmed in by the greatest difficulties, so that no means of preserving life seemed to remain. <note n="240"> <div sID="gen120817" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="el">Εξαπορεῖσθαι</foreign> properly signifies to be utterly at a stand, not knowing how to proceed. — In <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.88.8">Psalm 88:8</reference>, where David says — <hi type="italic">I am shut up, and I cannot come forth</hi>, the Hebrew words <foreign xml:lang="he"> ולא אצא</foreign>(<hi type="italic">velo etse</hi>,) are rendered in the Septuagint — <foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ οὐκ ἐξεπορευόμην</foreign> — <hi type="italic">and I could not come forth</hi>. It is worthy of notice that, in the metre version, the idea expressed by Calvin, as implied in the verb <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐξαπορεῖσθαι</foreign>, is fully brought out — “find no evasion for me.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120817" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120815" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120812" osisID="2Cor.1.8" type="section"/>
entries.68dee6c07f689d54c7527b4934317053456e2e84: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.9" sID="gen120818" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">Nay more, we had the sentence of death</hi> This is as though we should say — “I had already laid my account with dying, or had regarded it as a thing fixed.” He borrows, however, a similitude from those who are under sentence of death, and look for nothing but the hour when they are to die. At the same time he says, that this sentence had been pronounced by him upon himself, by which he intimates, that it was in his own view that he had been sentenced to death — that he might not seem to have had it from any revelation from God. In this <hi type="italic">sentence,</hi> <note n="241"> <div sID="gen120820" type="x-p"/> “The Greek word is <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀποςκριμα</foreign>, used here in this place only in the New Testament. [...] The most genuine translation is <hi type="italic">sentence</hi>; for so Hesychius expounds the word <foreign xml:lang="el">κατακριςμα </foreign>— <foreign xml:lang="el">ψὢφο</foreign>”, whom <hi type="italic">Favorinus</hi> followeth <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> in this, as in many other particulars. [...] The word then doth signifie a <hi type="italic">sentence</hi> passing upon him, <hi type="italic">that he must die</hi>. This he had received, but from whom? Not from God, for God delivered him; nor from the magistrate; there was no such decree that we read of against him. Therefore it was onely from his own feares, his own thoughts, which maketh him say — <hi type="italic">he had received it in himself</hi>. [...] God’s thoughts were other than Paul’s. Paul absolutely concluded he should die, but God had purposed the contrary.” — <hi type="italic">Burgesse</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120820" type="x-p"/> </note> therefore, there is something more implied than in the feeling of <hi type="italic">anxiety </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐξαπορεῖσθαι)</foreign> that he had made mention of, because in the former case there was despair of life, but in this case there is certain death. We must, however, take notice, chiefly, of what he adds as to the design — that he had been reduced to this extremity, <hi type="italic">that he might not trust in himself</hi> For I do not agree with what Chrysostom says — that the Apostle did not stand in need of such a remedy, but set himself forth to others as a pattern merely in appearance. <note n="242"> <div sID="gen120821" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il se propose aux autres comme pour exemple, non pas qu’il en fust ainsi quant à luy</foreign>;” — “He sets himself forth, as it were by way of example — not that it had been so as to himself.”<div eID="gen120821" type="x-p"/> </note> For he was a man that was <hi type="italic">subject, </hi>in other respects, <hi type="italic">to like passions </hi>as other men — (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jas.5.17">James 5:17</reference>) — not merely to cold and heat, but also to misdirected confidence, rashness, and the like. I do not say that he was addicted to these vices, but this I say, that he was capable of being tempted to them, and that this was the remedy that God seasonably interposed, that they might not make their way into his mind. <note n="243"> <div sID="gen120822" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De peur qu’ils ne saisissent plenement son esprit et son coeur</foreign>;” — “That they might not take full possession of his mind and his heart.”<div eID="gen120822" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120823" type="x-p"/>There are, accordingly, two things to be observed here. In the <hi type="italic">first </hi>place — that the fleshly confidence with which we are puffed up, is so obstinate, that it cannot be overthrown in any other way than by our falling into utter despair. <note n="244"> <div sID="gen120824" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sinon que nous tombions en telle extremite que nous ne voyons aucune esperance en nous</foreign>;” — “Except by our falling into such an extremity, that we see no hope in ourselves.”<div eID="gen120824" type="x-p"/> </note> For as the flesh is proud, it does not willingly give way, and never ceases to be insolent until it has been constrained; nor are we brought to true submission, until we have been brought down by the <hi type="italic">mighty hand of God. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.6">1 Peter 5:6</reference>.) <hi type="italic">Secondly, </hi>it is to be observed, that the saints themselves have some remains of this disease adhering to them, and that for this reason they are often reduced to an extremity, that, stript of all self-confidence, they may learn humility: nay more, that this malady is so deeply rooted in the minds of men, that even the most advanced are not thoroughly purged from it, until God sets death before their eyes. And hence we may infer, how displeasing to God confidence in ourselves must be, when for the purpose of correcting it, it is necessary that we should be condemned to death.<div eID="gen120823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120825" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But in God that raiseth the dead</hi> As we must first die, <note n="245"> <div sID="gen120826" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme il nous est necessaire premierement de venir comme à mourir</foreign>;” — “As we need first to come as it were to die”<div eID="gen120826" type="x-p"/> </note> in order that, renouncing confidence in ourselves, and conscious of our own weakness, we may claim no honor to ourselves, so even that were not sufficient, if we did not proceed a step farther. Let us begin, therefore, with despairing of ourselves, but with the view of placing our hope in God. Let us be brought low in ourselves, but in order that we may be raised up by his power. Paul, accordingly, having brought to nothing the pride of the flesh, immediately substitutes in its place a confidence that rests upon God.<hi type="italic"> Not in ourselves, </hi>says he,<hi type="italic"> but in God</hi><div eID="gen120825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120827" type="x-p"/>The epithet that follows, Paul has adapted to the connection of the subject, as he does in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.4.17">Romans 4:17</reference>, where he speaks of Abraham. For to<div eID="gen120827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120828" type="x-p"/>believe in God, who calleth those things that are not, as though they were, and to hope in God who raiseth the dead,<div eID="gen120828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120829" type="x-p"/>are equivalent to his setting before him as an object of contemplation, the power of God in creating his elect out of nothing, and raising up the dead. Hence Paul says, that death had been set before his eyes, that he might, in consequence of this, recognize the more distinctly the power of God, by which he had been raised up from the dead. The first thing in order, it is true, is this — that, by means of the strength with which God furnishes us, we should acknowledge him as the Author of life; but as in consequence of our dulness the light of life often dazzles our eyes, it is necessary that we should be brought to God by having death presented to our view. <note n="246"> <div sID="gen120830" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il nous est necessaire pour estre amenez à Dieu, d’estre reduits â telle extremite que nous voyons la mort presente deuant nos yeux</foreign>;” — “It is necessary, in order that we may be brought back to God, that we should be brought to such an extremity, that we see death presented before our eyes.”<div eID="gen120830" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120829" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120818" osisID="2Cor.1.9" type="section"/>
entries.fa2d3f070609dad0cd0827db69129b1a427f8c85: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.10" sID="gen120831" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">Who hath delivered us from so great a death</hi> Here he applies to himself personally, what he had stated in a general way, and by way of proclaiming the grace of God, he declares that he had not been disappointed in his expectation, inasmuch as he had been <hi type="italic">delivered from death, </hi>and that too, in no common form. As to his manner of expression, the hyperbole, which he makes use of, is not unusual in the Scriptures, for it frequently occurs, both in the Prophets and in the Psalms, and it is made use of even in common conversation. What Paul acknowledges as to himself personally, let every one now take home as applicable to himself.<div eID="gen120832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120833" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In whom we have an assured hope.</hi> He promises himself as to the future, also, that beneficence of God, which he had often experienced in the past. Nor is it without good reason; for the Lord, by accomplishing in part what he has promised, bids us hope well as to what remains. Nay more, in proportion to the number of favors that we receive from him, does he by so many pledges, or earnests, as it were, confirm his promises. <note n="247"> <div sID="gen120834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Granville Penn</hi> reads the passage as follows: “Who hath delivered us from so great a death; and will deliver us: in whom we hope that he will deliver us.” — “The <hi type="italic">Vat</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Ephrem</hi> MSS.” he observes, “read <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥύσεται, </foreign>not <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥύεται</foreign>, as in the <hi type="italic">rec</hi>. text. The latter reading seems to have been substituted, because <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥύσεται</foreign>, occurs again in the following sentence; but the Apostle repeats the word, that he may qualify it by <foreign xml:lang="el">ἠλπίκαμεν</foreign>, (we hope.”) — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120834" type="x-p"/> </note> Now, although Paul had no doubt that God would of his own accord be present with him, yet he exhorts the Corinthians to commend to God in their prayers his safety. For when he assumes it as certain, that he will be aided by them, this declaration has the force of an exhortation, and he means that they would not merely do it as a matter of duty, but also with advantage. <note n="248"> <div sID="gen120835" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais aussi auec bonne issue, d’autant qu’ils seront exaucez</foreign>;” — “But also with good success, inasmuch as they will be heard.”<div eID="gen120835" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120836" type="x-p"/>“Your prayers, also,” he says, “will help me.” <note n="249"> <div sID="gen120837" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’aide, dit il, que vous me feriez par vos prieres, ne sera point sans fruit</foreign>;” — “The aid, he says, that you will afford me by your prayers, will not be without advantage.”<div eID="gen120837" type="x-p"/> </note> For God wills not that the duty of mutual intercession, which he enjoins upon us, should be without advantage. This ought to be a stimulus to us, on the one hand, to solicit the intercession of our brethren, when we are weighed down by any necessity, and, on the other, to render similar assistance in return, since we are informed, that it is not only a duty that is well pleasing to God, but also profitable to ourselves. Nor is it owing to distrust that the Apostle implores the friendly aid of his brethren, <note n="250"> <div sID="gen120838" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">You also helping together by prayer for us,</hi> (<foreign xml:lang="el">Συνυπουργούντων καὶ ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τὣ δεήσει</foreign>.) The particle <foreign xml:lang="el">καί</foreign> is emphatical, <hi type="italic">You also</hi> — implying, that neither God’s promise, nor his power, would procure this mercy alone without their prayer. Besides the goodness of God on his part, there must be prayer on their part. The word in the original for helping is emphatical, being twice compounded. <foreign xml:lang="el">̔υπουργούντων</foreign> doth denote the <hi type="italic">service</hi> and <hi type="italic">ministry</hi> of those who are <hi type="italic">under</hi> us; and so it doth imply, that the Church doth owe as a debt unto their spiritual guides earnest prayer for them. [...] Then there is the preposition <foreign xml:lang="el">σύν</foreign> added, which doth denote not only their effectual prayers, but their <hi type="italic">concord</hi> and <hi type="italic">agreement</hi> therein, and that in their public and solemn assemblies. Again, the word signifying — to <hi type="italic">work</hi>, and <hi type="italic">labor</hi>, doth denote what the nature of prayer is — that the soul labors therein, is fervent, full of agonies; which showeth that the customary formal prayers of most people are not worthy of the name: there is no <hi type="italic">labor</hi>, or fervency of the soul therein. — They labored by <hi type="italic">prayer</hi>. They did not labor by using friends to solicit the magistrate in Paul’s behalf, for there was no hope from them, but they made their addresses to God.” — <hi type="italic">Burgesse</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120838" type="x-p"/> </note> for, while he felt assured, that his safety would be the object of God’s care, <note n="251"> <div sID="gen120839" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que Dieu auroit soin de son salut et proufit</foreign>;” — “That God would take care of his safety and advantage.”<div eID="gen120839" type="x-p"/> </note> though he were destitute of all human help, yet he knew that it was well pleasing to God, that he should be aided by the prayers of the saints. He had respect, also, to the promises that were given, that assistance of this kind would not be in vain. Hence, in order that he might not overlook any assistance that was appointed to him by God, he desired that the brethren should pray for his preservation.<div eID="gen120836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120840" type="x-p"/>The sum is this — that we follow the word of God, that is, that we obey his commandments and cleave to his promises. This is not the part of those who have recourse to the assistance of the dead; <note n="252"> <div sID="gen120841" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui out leurs recours aux prieres des saincts trespassez</foreign>;” — “Who have recourse to the prayers of departed saints.”<div eID="gen120841" type="x-p"/> </note> for not contented with the sources of help appointed by God, they call in to their aid a new one, that has no countenance from any declaration of Scripture. For whatever we find mentioned there as to mutual intercession, has no reference to the dead, but is expressly restricted to the living. Hence Papists act childishly in perverting those passages, so as to give some colour to their superstition. <note n="253"> <div sID="gen120842" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour desguiser et farder leur superstition</foreign>;” — “To disguise and color over their superstition.”<div eID="gen120842" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120840" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120831" osisID="2Cor.1.10" type="section"/>
entries.ee799ee5ddada4493e529b7fcdc8746bc0de5b40:
11. That the gift bestowed upon us through means of many persons. As there is some difficulty in Paul’s words, interpreters differ as to the meaning. I shall not spend time in setting aside the interpretations of others, nor indeed is there any need for this, provided only we are satisfied as to the true and proper meaning. He had said, that the prayers of the Corinthians would be an assistance to him. He now adds a second advantage that would accrue from it — a higher manifestation of God’s glory. “For whatever God will confer upon me,” says he, “being as it were obtained through means of many persons, will, also, by many be celebrated with praises:” or in this way — “Many will give thanks to God in my behalf, because, in affording help to me, he has favorably regarded the prayers, not merely of one but of many.” In the first place, while it is our duty to allow no favor from God to pass without rendering praise, it becomes us, nevertheless, more especially when our prayers have been favorably regarded by him, to acknowledge his mercy with thanksgiving, as he commands us to do in Psalm 50:15. Nor ought this to be merely where our own personal interest is concerned, but also where the welfare of the Church in general, or that of any one of our brethren is involved. Hence when we mutually pray one for another, and obtain our desire, the glory of God is so much the more set forth, inasmuch as we all acknowledge, with thanksgiving, God’s benefits — both those that are conferred publicly upon the whole Church, and also those that are bestowed privately upon individuals.
In this interpretation there is nothing forced; for as to the circumstance that in the Greek the article being introduced between the two clauses by many persons, and the gift conferred upon me appears to disjoin them,
“Car à suyure l’ordre du texte Grec il y auroit ainsi mot à mot, Afin que de plusieurs personnes, à nous le don conferé, par plusieurs soit recognu en action de graces pour nous;” — “For, following the order of the Greek text, it would be literally thus: In order that from many persons the gift conferred upon us, may by many be acknowledged with thanksgiving on our account.”
that has no force, as it is frequently found introduced between clauses that are connected with each other. Here, however, it is with propriety introduced in place of an adversative particle;
“En lieu de quelque article aduersative qu’on appelle, comme Toutesfois ou Neantmoins;” — “In place of some adversative particle, as it is called, as for example, Notwithstanding or Nevertheless.”
for although it had come forth from many persons, it was nevertheless peculiar to Paul. To take the phrase διὰ πολλῶν (by means of many) in the neuter gender,
“De rapporter ce mot Par plusieurs, aux choses;” — “To take this phrase, By means of many, as referring to things.”
as some do, is at variance with the connection of the passage.
It may, however, be asked, why he says From many persons, rather than From many men, and what is the meaning of the term person here? I answer, it is as though he had said — With respect to many. For the favor was conferred upon Paul in such a way, that it might be given to many. Hence, as God had respect to many, he says on that account, that many persons were the cause of it. Some Greek manuscripts have ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν — on your account; and although this appears to be at variance with Paul’s design, and the connection of the words, it may, nevertheless, be explained with propriety in this manner: “When God shall have heard you in behalf of my welfare, and that too for your own welfare, thanks will be given by many on your account.”
2 Corinthians 1:12-14
12. For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
12. Nam gloriatio nostra haec est: testimonium conscientiae nostrae, quod in simplicitate et puritate
“Purete, ou, integrite;” — “Purity, or integrity.”
Dei, non in sapientia carnali, sed in gratia Dei versati sumus in mundo; abundantius autem erga vos.
13. For we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge; and I trust ye shall acknowledge even to the end;
13. Non enim alia scribimus vobis quam quae recognoscitis vel etiam agnoscitis: spero autem, quod usque in finem agnoscetis:
14. As also ye have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.
14. Quemadmodum et agnovistis nos ex parte: siquidem gloriatio vestra sumus: sicuti et vos nostra in die Domini Iesu.
entries.6b72fea288f0e3602c973600842cf1c045121abf: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.12" sID="gen120860" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">For our glorying is this.</hi> He assigns a reason why his preservation should be a subject of interest to all — that he had conducted himself <note n="258"> <div sID="gen120862" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">We have had our conversation</hi> (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀνεστράφημεν</foreign>.) The verb <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀναστρέφω</foreign>, is compounded of <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀνὰ</foreign>, again, and <foreign xml:lang="el">στρέφω</foreign>, to turn — a continual coming back again to the point from which he set out — a circulation — beginning, continuing, and ending everything to the glory of God; setting out with divine views, and still maintaining them; beginning in the Spirit, and ending in the Spirit; acting in reference to God, as the <hi type="italic">planets</hi> do in reference to the <hi type="italic">sun</hi>, deriving all their light, heat, and motion from him; and incessantly and regularly revolving round him. Thus acted Paul: thus acted the primitive Christians; and thus must every Christian act who expects to see God in his glory.” — <hi type="italic">Dr. Adam Clarke</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120862" type="x-p"/> </note> among them all in<hi type="italic"> simplicity and sincerity</hi> He deserved, therefore, to be dear to them, and it would have been very unfeeling not to be concerned in reference to such a servant of the Lord, that he might be long preserved for the benefit of the Church. “I have conducted myself before all in such a manner, that it is no wonder if I have the approbation and love of all good men.” He takes occasion from this, however, for the sake of those to whom he was writing, to make a digression for the purpose of declaring his own integrity. As, however, it is not enough to be approved of by man’s judgment, and as Paul himself was harassed by the unjust and malignant judgments of some, or rather by corrupt and blind attachments, <note n="259"> <div sID="gen120863" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par les affections qu’ils portoyent à d’autres pour des raisons friuoles, et quasi sans scauoir pourquoy</foreign>;” — “By attachments that they cherished towards others on trivial grounds, and in a manner without knowing why.”<div eID="gen120863" type="x-p"/> </note> he adduces his own conscience as his witness — which is all one as though he had cited God as a witness, or had made what he says matter of appeal to his tribunal.<div eID="gen120861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120864" type="x-p"/>But how does Paul’s glorying in his integrity comport with that statement,<div eID="gen120864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120865" type="x-p"/>He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord?<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.17">2 Corinthians 10:17</reference>.)<div eID="gen120865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120866" type="x-p"/>Besides, who is so upright <note n="260"> <div sID="gen120867" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui est celuy, tant pur et entier soit il</foreign>?” — “Where is the man, be he ever so pure and perfect?”<div eID="gen120867" type="x-p"/> </note> as to dare to boast in the presence of God? In the first place, Paul does not oppose himself to God, as though he had anything that was his own, or that was from himself. Farther, he does not place the foundation of his salvation in that integrity to which he lays claim, nor does he make confidence in <hi type="italic">that </hi>the ground of his dependence. Lastly, he does not glory in God’s gifts in such a way as not at the same time to render all the glory to him as their sole Author, and ascribe everything to him. <note n="261"> <div sID="gen120868" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et rapporte toutes choses a sa bonte</foreign>;” — “And ascribes everything to his goodness.”<div eID="gen120868" type="x-p"/> </note> These three exceptions lay a foundation for every godly person glorying on good grounds in all God’s benefits; while the wicked, on the other hand, cannot glory even in God, except on false and improper grounds. Let us therefore, first of all, acknowledge ourselves to be indebted to God for everything good that we possess, claiming no merit to ourselves. Secondly, let us hold fast this foundation — that our dependence for salvation be grounded exclusively on the mercy of God. Lastly, let us repose ourselves <note n="262"> <div sID="gen120869" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Arrestons nous et reposons du tout</foreign>;” — “Let us stay ourselves, and wholly repose.”<div eID="gen120869" type="x-p"/> </note> in the sole author of every blessing. Then in that there will be a pious <note n="263"> <div sID="gen120870" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Bonne et saincte</foreign>;” — “Good and holy.”<div eID="gen120870" type="x-p"/> </note> glorying in every kind of blessing.<div eID="gen120866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120871" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That in the simplicity</hi> <note n="264"> <div sID="gen120872" type="x-p"/> “The most ancient MSS. read <foreign xml:lang="el">ἁγιοτητι</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">holiness</hi>) — not <foreign xml:lang="el">ἁπλοτητι</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">simplicity</hi>.)” — <hi type="italic">Penn</hi><div eID="gen120872" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">of God.</hi> He employs the expression <hi type="italic">simplicity of God </hi>here, in the same way as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.23">Romans 3:23</reference>, <hi type="italic">the glory of God; </hi>and in <reference osisRef="Bible:John.12.43">John 12:43</reference>, <hi type="italic">the glory of God and of men. </hi>Those who love the <hi type="italic">glory of men, </hi>wish to appear something before men, or to stand well in the opinion of men. The <hi type="italic">glory of God</hi> is what a man has in the sight of God. Hence Paul does not reckon it enough to declare that his sincerity was perceived by men, but adds, that he was such in the sight of God. <foreign xml:lang="el">Εἰλικρινείᾳ </foreign>(which I have rendered <hi type="italic">purity</hi>) is closely connected with <hi type="italic">simplicity; </hi>for it is an open and upright way of acting, such as makes a man’s heart as it were transparent. <note n="265"> <div sID="gen120873" type="x-p"/> “The word used here <foreign xml:lang="el">εἰλικρινείᾳ</foreign> and rendered <hi type="italic">sincerity</hi> — denotes properly — <hi type="italic">clearness</hi>, such as is judged of or discerned in sunshine, (<foreign xml:lang="el">εἴλη</foreign>, <hi type="italic">sunshine</hi>, and <foreign xml:lang="el">κρίνω</foreign>, to <hi type="italic">judge</hi>,) and thence pureness, integrity. It is most probable that the <hi type="italic">phrase</hi> here denotes that sincerity which God produces and approves; and the sentiment is, that pure religion, the religion of God, produces entire sincerity in the heart. Its purposes and aims are open and manifest, <hi type="italic">as if seen in the sunshine</hi>. The plans of the world are obscure, deceitful, and dark, <hi type="italic">as if in the night</hi>.” — <hi type="italic">Barnes</hi>. The same term is made use of by Paul in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.5.8">1 Cor. 5:8</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.2.17">2 Corinthians 2:17</reference> On comparing the various instances in which this term is employed by the Apostle, we have occasion to observe the admirable harmony between his exhortations and practice. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120873" type="x-p"/> </note> Both terms stand opposed to craft, deception, and all underhand schemes.<div eID="gen120871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120874" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Not in fleshly wisdom.</hi> There is here a sort of anticipation; for what might be felt to be wanting in him he readily acknowledges, nay more, he openly proclaims, that he is destitute of, but adds, that he is endowed with what is incomparably more excellent — the <hi type="italic">grace of God</hi> “I acknowledge,” says he, “that I am destitute of <hi type="italic">fleshly wisdom, </hi>but I have been furnished with divine influence, and if any one is not satisfied with <hi type="italic">that, </hi>he is at liberty to depreciate my Apostleship. If, on the other hand, <hi type="italic">fleshly wisdom </hi>is of no value, then I want nothing that is not fitted to secure well-grounded praise.” He gives the name of <hi type="italic">fleshly wisdom </hi>to everything apart from Christ, that procures for us the reputation of <hi type="italic">wisdom. </hi>See the <hi type="italic">first and</hi> <hi type="italic">second </hi>chapters of the former epistle. Hence, by the grace of God, which is contrasted with it, we must understand everything that transcends man’s nature and capacity, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which openly manifested the power of God in the weakness of the flesh.<div eID="gen120874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120875" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">More abundantly towards you</hi> Not that he had been less upright elsewhere, but that he had remained longer at Corinth, in order that he might (not to mention other purposes) afford a fuller and clearer proof of his integrity. He has, however, expressed himself intentionally in such a way as to intimate that he did not require evidences that were far-fetched, inasmuch as they were themselves the best witnesses of all that he had said.<div eID="gen120875" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120860" osisID="2Cor.1.12" type="section"/>
entries.53091bde16608da59c05b45b896e69ea11f7eaeb: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.13" sID="gen120876" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">For we write no other things</hi> Here he indirectly reproves the false apostles, who recommended themselves by immoderate boastings, while they had little or no ground for it; and at the same time he obviates calumnies, in order that no one may object, that he claims for himself more than is his due. He says, therefore, that he does not in words boast of anything that he is not prepared to make good by deeds, and that, too, from the testimony of the Corinthians.<div eID="gen120877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120878" type="x-p"/>The ambiguity, however, of the words, has given occasion for this passage being misinterpreted. <foreign xml:lang="el">Αναγινώσκειν,</foreign> among the Greeks, signifies sometimes <hi type="italic">to read, </hi>and at other times <hi type="italic">to recognize. </hi><foreign xml:lang="el">Επιγινώσκειν </foreign>sometimes signifies <hi type="italic">to discover, </hi>while at other times it means what the Latins properly express by the verb <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">agnoscere</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>to <hi type="italic">own, </hi>as among lawyers the phrase is used to <hi type="italic">own a child</hi>, <note n="266"> <div sID="gen120879" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce que disons <hi type="italic">Auouer</hi>: comme on dira <hi type="italic">Auouer vn enfant</hi></foreign>;” — “What we express by the verb to own, as when you speak of <hi type="italic">owning a child</hi>.”<div eID="gen120879" type="x-p"/> </note> as Budaeus also has observed. In this way <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπιγινώσκειν </foreign>means more than <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀναγινώσκειν</foreign> For we say that a person <hi type="italic">recognises </hi>a thing, that is, that being silently convinced of it in his judgment, he perceives it to be true, while at the same time he does not <hi type="italic">acknowledge </hi>it, or, in other words, cordially intimate his assent to it.<div eID="gen120878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120880" type="x-p"/>Let us now examine Paul’s words. Some read thus — <hi type="italic">We write no other things than what ye read and acknowledge, </hi>which it is very manifest is exceedingly lifeless, not to say senseless. For as to Ambrose’s qualifying the statement in this way — <hi type="italic">You not only read, but also acknowledge, </hi>there is no one that does not perceive that it is quite foreign to the import of the words. And the meaning that I have stated is plain, and hangs together naturally, and, up to this point, there is nothing to prevent readers from understanding it, were it not that they have had their eyes shut, from being misled by the different meanings of the word. The sum is this — that Paul declares, that he brings forward no other things than what were known and perceived by the Corinthians — nay more, things as to which they would bear him witness. The first term employed is <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">recognoscere</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>(to <hi type="italic">recognize,) </hi>which is applicable, when persons are convinced from experience that matters are so. The second is <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">agnoscere</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>(to <hi type="italic">acknowledge,) </hi>meaning that they give their assent to the truth. <note n="267"> <div sID="gen120881" type="x-p"/> The word <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀςναγινώσκετε</foreign>, “properly means to <hi type="italic">know accurately</hi>, to <hi type="italic">distinguish</hi>. It is probably used here in the sense of knowing accurately or surely, of <hi type="italic">recognizing</hi> from their former acquaintance with him.” <foreign xml:lang="el">᾿Επιγινώσκειν</foreign> “here means that they would <hi type="italic">fully recognize</hi>, or know entirely to their satisfaction, that the sentiments which he here expressed were such as accorded with his general manner of life.” — <hi type="italic">Barnes</hi>. Dr. Bloomfield, who approves of the view taken by Calvin of the meaning of the verb <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀναγινώσκετε</foreign>, remarks, that the word is employed in the same sense by Xenophon. Anab., 5:8, 6, as well as elsewhere in the Classical writers. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120881" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120882" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And, I hope, will acknowledge even to the end.</hi> As the Corinthians had not yet perfectly returned to a sound mind, so as to be prepared to weigh his fidelity in a just and even balance, <note n="268"> <div sID="gen120883" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est à dire, pour en iuger droitement</foreign>;” — “That is to say, to judge of it aright.”<div eID="gen120883" type="x-p"/> </note> but at the same time had begun to abate somewhat of their perverse and malignant judgment respecting him, he intimates, that he hopes better as to the future. “You have already,” says he, “to some extent acknowledged me. I hope that you will acknowledge more and more what I have been among you, and in what manner I have conducted myself.” <note n="269"> <div sID="gen120884" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que vous cognoistrez de plus en plus comme i’ay conversé entre vous, et comme ie m’y suis gouuerné, et ainsi auouërez ce que maintenant i’en di</foreign>;” — “That you will acknowledge more and more how I have conducted myself among you, and how I have regulated myself, and thus you will assent to what I now say.”<div eID="gen120884" type="x-p"/> </note> From this it appears more clearly what he meant by the word <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπιγινώσκειν</foreign>. (<hi type="italic">acknowledge</hi> <note n="270"> <div sID="gen120885" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que c’est qu’il a entendu par le dernier des deux mots desquels nous auons parler, lequel nous auons traduit <hi type="italic">Auouer</hi></foreign>;” — “What it was that he meant by the last of the two words of which we have spoken, which we have rendered — <hi type="italic">Acknowledge</hi>.<div eID="gen120885" type="x-p"/> </note> ) Now this relates to a season of repentance, for they had at the beginning acknowledged him fully and thoroughly; afterwards their right judgment had been beclouded <note n="271"> <div sID="gen120886" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Obscurci et abbastardi en eux par les propos obliques des faux — Apostres et autres malins</foreign>;” — “Obscured and corrupted by the unfair statements of the false Apostles, and other malicious persons.”<div eID="gen120886" type="x-p"/> </note> by unfair statements, but they had at length begun to return in part to a sound mind.<div eID="gen120882" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120876" osisID="2Cor.1.13" type="section"/>
entries.ef37d2a9d599c5d63e6c0284cf5523d37a64423b:
14. For we are your glorying. We have briefly adverted to the manner in which it is allowable for saints to glory in God’s benefits — when they repose themselves in God alone, and have no other object of aim. Thus it was a ground of pious glorying on the part of Paul, that he had, by his ministry, brought the Corinthians under obedience to Christ; and of the Corinthians, on the other hand, that they had been trained up so faithfully and so virtuously by such an Apostle — a privilege that had not been allotted to all. This way of glorying in men does not stand in the way of our glorying in God alone. Now he instructs the Corinthians, that it is of the greatest importance for themselves that they should acknowledge him to be a faithful, and not a merely pretended, servant of Christ; because, in the event of their withdrawing from him, they would deprive themselves of the highest glory. In these words he reproves their fickleness, inasmuch as they voluntarily deprived themselves of the highest glory, by listening too readily to the spiteful and envious.
In the day of the Lord By this I understand the last day, which will put an end to all the fleeting
“Vaines et caduques;” — “Empty and fading.”
glories of this world. He means, then, that the glorying of which he is now speaking is not evanescent, as those things are that glitter in the eyes of men, but is abiding and stable, inasmuch as it will remain until the day of Christ. For then will Paul enjoy the triumph of the many victories that he had obtained under Christ’s auspices, and will lead forth in splendor all the nations that have, by means of his ministry, been brought under Christ’s glorious yoke; and the Church of the Corinthians will glory in having been founded and trained up by the services of so distinguished an Apostle.
2 Corinthians 1:15-20
15. And in this confidence I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit;
15. Et hac fiducia volui primum ad vos venire, ut secundam
“Seconde, ou double;” — “Second, or double.”
gratiam haberetis,
16. And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judaea.
16. Et per vos transire in Macedoniam:
The Latin text "et per vos transire in Macedoniam:" in the original manuscript was at the end of verse 15, I have moved it to match the Vulgate (possible error in the Edinburgh edition.) — fj.
et rursum e Macedonia venire ad vos, et a vobis deduci in Iudaeam.
17. When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay?
17. Hoc igitur quum animo propositum haberem, nuncubi levitate usus sum? aut quae cogito, secundum carnem cogito? ut sit apud me Etiam, etiam: et Non, non.
18. But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay.
18. Fidelis Deus, quod sermo noster apud vos non fuit Etiam et non.
19. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea.
19. Dei enim Filius Iesus Christus in vobis per nos praedicatus, per me, et Silvanum, et Timotheum, non fuit Etiam et non: sed Etiam fuit in ipso.
20. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.
20. Quaecunque enim sunt Dei promissiones, in illo sunt Etiam: quare et per ipsum sit Amen Deo ad gloriam per nos.
entries.bae932bb6a5bf2288eb568ce6fd65f4edd13d20e: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.15" sID="gen120908" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">In this confidence.</hi> After having given them reason to expect that he would come, he had subsequently changed his intention. This was made an occasion of calumny against him, as appears from the excuse that he brings forward. When he says that it was from relying on<hi type="italic"> this confidence </hi>that he formed the purpose of coming to them, he indirectly throws the blame upon the Corinthians, inasmuch as they had, by their ingratitude, hindered, to some extent, his coming to them, by depriving him of <hi type="italic">that confidence.</hi><div eID="gen120909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120910" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That ye might have a second benefit</hi> The first benefit had been this — that he had devoted himself for the entire period of <hi type="italic">a year and six months </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.11">Acts 18:11</reference>) to the work of gaining them to the Lord; the <hi type="italic">second </hi>was their being confirmed, by means of his coming to them, in the faith which they had once received, and being stirred up by his sacred admonitions to make farther progress. Of this latter benefit the Corinthians had deprived themselves, inasmuch as they had not allowed the apostle to come to them. They were paying, therefore, the penalty of their own fault, and they had no ground for imputing any blame to Paul. If any one, however, prefers, with Chrysostom, to take <foreign xml:lang="el">χάριν</foreign> <hi type="italic">(benefit) </hi>as used instead of <foreign xml:lang="el">καράν</foreign><hi type="italic">, (joy,) </hi>I do not much object to it. <note n="275"> <div sID="gen120911" type="x-p"/> “Most modern Commentators explain the <foreign xml:lang="el">χάριν</foreign> <hi type="italic">gift</hi> or <hi type="italic">benefit</hi>; but the ancient Commentators, and some modern ones, as Wolf and Schleus, <hi type="italic">gratification</hi> for <foreign xml:lang="el">χαράν</foreign>. It should seem to mean <hi type="italic">benefit</hi> generally, every spiritual advantage, or gratification from his society, imparted by his presence.” — <hi type="italic">Bloomfield</hi> <hi type="italic">One</hi> MS. reads <foreign xml:lang="el">χαράν</foreign> <hi type="italic">Kypke</hi>, who renders <foreign xml:lang="el">χάριν</foreign>, joy adduces instances in support of this meaning of <foreign xml:lang="el">χάρι</foreign>”, though acknowledged to be unusual, from <hi type="italic">Plutarch</hi>, <hi type="italic">Polybius</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Euripides</hi>. The phrase is rendered in Tyndale’s version, (1534,) and also in Cranmer’s, (1539,) and Geneva, (1557,) versions — <hi type="italic">one pleasure moare</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120911" type="x-p"/> </note> The former interpretation, however, is more simple.<div eID="gen120910" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120908" osisID="2Cor.1.15" type="section"/>
entries.86539cd8d8d2f77dc4b6f1b0f4909ea5798f1961: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.17" sID="gen120912" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">Did I use fickleness?</hi> There are two things, more especially, that prevent the purposes of men from being carried into effect, or their promises from being faithfully performed. The one is that they make changes upon them almost every hour, and the other is that they are too rash in forming their plans. It is a sign of changeableness to purpose or promise what you almost immediately afterwards regret. With that fault Paul declares he had not been chargeable. “I have not,” says he, “through <hi type="italic">fickleness </hi>drawn back from the promise that I made.” He declares also that he had been on his guard against rashness and misdirected confidence; for such is the way in which I explain the expression — <hi type="italic">purpose according to the flesh</hi> For it is, as I have stated, the common practice of men, as though they were not dependent on God’s providence, and were not subject to his will, to determine rashly and presumptuously what they will do. Now God, with the view of punishing this presumption, defeats their plans, so as to prevent them from having a prosperous issue, and in many instances holds up themselves to ridicule.<div eID="gen120913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120914" type="x-p"/>The expression, it is true, <hi type="italic">according to the flesh, </hi>might be extended farther, so as to include all wicked schemes, and such as are not directed to a right end, as for example such as are dictated by ambition, avarice, or any other depraved affection. Paul, however, in my opinion, did not intend here to refer to any thing of that nature, but merely to reprove that rashness which is but too customary on the part of man, and in daily use in the forming of plans. To <hi type="italic">purpose, </hi>therefore, <hi type="italic">according to the flesh, </hi>is not owning God as our ruler, but, instead of this, being impelled by a rash presumption, which is afterwards justly derided by God, and punished. The apostle, with the view of clearing himself from these faults, proposes a question, as if in the person of his opponents. Hence it is probable, as I have already said, that some unfavorable report had been put in circulation by wicked persons.<div eID="gen120914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120915" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That with me there should be yea, yea</hi> Some connect this statement with what goes before, and explain it thus: “As if it were in my power to perform whatever I purpose, as men determine that they will do whatever comes into their mind, and <hi type="italic">order their ways, </hi>as Solomon speaks, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Prov.16.1">Proverbs 16:1</reference>,) while they cannot so much as govern their tongue.” And, undoubtedly, the words seem to imply this much — that what has been once affirmed must remain fixed, and what has been once denied must never be done. So James in his Epistle (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jas.5.12">James 5:12</reference>) says,<div eID="gen120915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120916" type="x-p"/>Let your yea be yea, and your nay nay, lest ye fall into dissimulation.<div eID="gen120916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120917" type="x-p"/>Farther, the context would in this way suit exceedingly well as to what goes before. For to <hi type="italic">purpose according to the flesh</hi> is this — when we wish that, without any exception, our determinations shall be like oracles. <note n="276"> <div sID="gen120918" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que nos deliberations et conseils soyent comme oracles et reuelations Diuines</foreign>;” — “That our purposes and plans shall be like oracles and Divine revelations.”<div eID="gen120918" type="x-p"/> </note> This interpretation, However, does not accord with what immediately <hi type="italic">follows</hi> — <hi type="italic">God is faithful, </hi>etc., where Paul makes use of the same form of expression, when he has it in view to intimate, that he had not been unfaithful in his preaching. Now it were absurd, if almost in the same verse he reckoned it as a fault that his yea should be yea, and his nay nay, and yet at the same time laid claim to it as his highest praise. I am aware of what could be said in reply, if any one were disposed to sport himself with subtleties, but I have no relish for anything that is not solid.<div eID="gen120917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120919" type="x-p"/>I have, therefore, no doubt, that in these words Paul designed to reprove fickleness, although they may seem to be susceptible of another meaning, for the purpose of clearing himself from that calumny — that he was accustomed to promise in words what he failed to perform in deeds. <note n="277"> <div sID="gen120920" type="x-p"/> “He (the apostle) anticipates and repels a reproach of <foreign xml:lang="el">ἰλαφρία</foreign>, or ‘<hi type="italic">lightness of purpose</hi>,’ in that change of mind, as if he was ‘<hi type="italic">a yea and nay man</hi>,’ (Shaksp.), on whose word no secure reliance could be placed. In the next verse he calls God to witness that his word to them was not, ‘<hi type="italic">both yea and nay</hi>;’ and in the beginning of the following chapter, he explains to them, that it was for their sakes that he abstained from executing his first intention.” — <hi type="italic">Penn</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120920" type="x-p"/> </note> Thus the reiterating of the affirmation and negation will not have the same meaning as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.37">Matthew 5:37</reference> and in James, but will bear this meaning — “that <hi type="italic">yea</hi> should with me be in this instance <hi type="italic">yea, </hi>and on the other hand, when it pleases me, <hi type="italic">nay, nay</hi> ” At the same time it is possible that it may have crept in through the ignorance of transcribers, as the old translation does not redouble the words, <note n="278"> <div sID="gen120921" type="x-p"/> The rendering of the Vulgate is as follows: “<foreign xml:lang="la">Ut sit apud me <hi type="italic">est</hi> et non</foreign>;” — “That with me there should be <hi type="italic">yea</hi> and <hi type="italic">nay</hi>.” This reading — <foreign xml:lang="el">τὸ ναὶ καὶ τὸ οὔ</foreign>, (yea and nay), is found in one Greek MS., as stated by Semler. Wiclif, (1380,) following the Vulgate, reads — “that at me, be <hi type="italic">it is</hi> and <hi type="italic">it is not</hi>.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120921" type="x-p"/> </note> However this may be, we ought not to be very solicitous as to the words, provided we are in possession of the apostle’s intention, which, as I have said, clearly appears from what follows. <note n="279"> <div sID="gen120922" type="x-p"/> “It was a proverbial manner among the Jews (see Wet.) of characterizing a man of strict probity and good faith, by saying, ‘his <hi type="italic">yes</hi> is <hi type="italic">yes</hi>, and his <hi type="italic">no</hi> is <hi type="italic">no’</hi> — that is, you may depend upon his word; as he declares, so it is; and as he promises, so he will do. Our Lord is therefore to be considered here (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.37">Matthew 5:37</reference>) not as prescribing the precise terms wherein we are to affirm or deny; in which case it would have suited better the simplicity of his style to say barely <foreign xml:lang="el">ναὶ καὶ οὔ</foreign> (<hi type="italic">yea and nay</hi>,) without doubling the words; but as enjoining such an habitual and inflexible regard to truth, as would render swearing unnecessary. That this manner of converting these adverbs into nouns, is in the idiom of the sacred penmen, we have another instance, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.20">2 Corinthians 1:20</reference>,) ‘For all the promises of God in him are <hi type="italic">yea</hi>, and in him <hi type="italic">Amen</hi>.’ (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ναὶ καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ἀμὴν</foreign>) — that is, <hi type="italic">certain</hi> and <hi type="italic">infallible</hi> truths. It is indeed a common idiom of the Greek tongue, to turn by means of the article any of the parts of speech ‘into a noun.” — <hi type="italic">Campbell on the Gospels</hi>, volume 2. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120922" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120919" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120912" osisID="2Cor.1.17" type="section"/>
entries.8084b26f849742a1291beda3dc8a7dd52052ae7b: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.18" sID="gen120923" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> <hi type="italic">God is faithful.</hi> By the term <hi type="italic">word</hi> he means doctrine, as is manifest from the reason that he adds, when he says, that the <hi type="italic">Son of God, who is preached by him, is not variable, etc.</hi> As to his being always consistent with himself in point of doctrine, and not differing from himself, <note n="280"> <div sID="gen120925" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">N’a point dit l’vn, puis l’autre</foreign>;” — “Does not say one thing and then another.”<div eID="gen120925" type="x-p"/> </note> he intends that by this they shall form a judgment as to his integrity, and in this way he removes every unfavorable suspicion of fickleness or unfaithfulness. It does not, however, necessarily follow, that the man who is faithful in doctrine, is also observant of truth in all his <hi type="italic">words. </hi>But as Paul did not reckon it of much importance in what estimation he was held, provided only the majesty of his doctrine remained safe and sound, he, on that account, calls the attention of the Corinthians chiefly to that matter. He intimates, it is true, that he observed in his whole life the same course of fidelity, as the Corinthians had seen in his ministry. He seems, however, as if intentionally, in repelling the calumny, to transfer it from his person to his doctrine, because he was unwilling that his apostleship should be indirectly defamed, while he was not greatly concerned as to himself in other respects.<div eID="gen120924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120926" type="x-p"/>But observe, with what zeal he applies himself to this. For he calls God to witness, how simple and pure his preaching was — not ambiguous, not variable, not temporizing. In his oath, too, he connects the truth of God with the truth of his doctrine. “The truth of my preaching is as sure and stable as God is faithful and true.” Nor is this to be wondered at, for the word of God, which Isaiah says <hi type="italic">endureth for ever, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.8">Isaiah 40:8</reference>,) is no other than what prophets and apostles published to the world, as Peter explains it. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.25">1 Peter 1:25</reference>.) Hence, too, his confidence <note n="281"> <div sID="gen120927" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De là vient aussi que S. Paul est bien si hardi</foreign>;” — “Hence, too, it comes that St. Paul is so very bold.”<div eID="gen120927" type="x-p"/> </note> in denouncing a curse upon angels, if they dared to bring another gospel, one that was at variance with his. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.8">Galatians 1:8</reference>.) Who would dare to make the angels of heaven subject to his doctrine, if he had not God as his authority and defense? With such an assurance of a good conscience does it become ministers <note n="282"> <div sID="gen120928" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et annonciateurs de la parolle de Dieu</foreign>;” — “And heralds of the word of God.”<div eID="gen120928" type="x-p"/> </note> to be endowed, who mount the pulpit to speak the word in Christ’s name — so as to feel assured that their doctrine can no more be overthrown than God himself.<div eID="gen120926" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120923" osisID="2Cor.1.18" type="section"/>
entries.7bfdbc64def16d3f38d74d60aa309c6b052627f3:
19. For the Son of God Here we have the proof — because his preaching
“Il dit donc que sa parolle n’a point este oui et non, c’est à dire variable; pource que sa predication,” etc.; — “He says, then, that his word had not been yea and nay, that is to say, variable; because his preaching,” etc.
contained nothing but Christ alone, who is the eternal and immutable truth of God. The clause preached by us is emphatic. For, as it may be, and often does happen, that Christ is disfigured by the inventions
“Et mensonges;” — “And fallacies.”
of men, and is adulterated, as it were, by their disguises, he declares that it had not been so as to himself or his associates, but that he had sincerely and with an integrity that was befitting, held forth Christ pure and undisguised. Why it is that he makes no mention of Apollos, while he mentions by name Timotheus and Silvanus, does not exactly appear; unless the reason be, as is probable, that the more that individuals were assailed by the calumnies of the wicked,
“Des calomniateurs et mesdisans;” — “By calumniators and slanderers.”
he was so much the more careful to defend them.
In these words, however, he intimates that his whole doctrine was summed up in a simple acquaintance with Christ alone, as in reality the whole of the gospel is included in it. Hence those go beyond due limits, who teach anything else than Christ alone, with whatever show of wisdom they may otherwise be puffed up. For as he is the end of the law, (Romans 10:4,) so he is the head — the sum — in fine, the consummation — of all spiritual doctrine.
In the second place, he intimates that his doctrine respecting Christ had not been variable, or ambiguous, so as to present him from time to time in a new shape after the manner of Proteus;
“En sorte qu’il l’ait transfiguré, maintenant en vne sorte, tantost en vne autre, comme les Poëtes disent que Proteus se transformoit en diuerses sortes;” — “So as to present him in different shapes, now in one form, then in another, as the poets say that Proteus transformed himself into different shapes.” The following poets (among others) make mention of the “shape — changing” Proteus: — Virgil, (Georg. 4:387); Ovid, (Met. 8:730); Horace, (Sat. 2:3, 71, Ep. I. 1:90.) See Calvin on John, vol. 2, p. 256, n. 1. — Ed.
as some persons make it their sport to make changes upon him,
“En toutes manieres;” — “In every way.”
just as if they were tossing a ball to and fro with their hand, simply for the purpose of displaying their dexterity. Others, with a view to procure the favor of men, present him under various forms, while there is still another class, that inculcate one day what on the next they retract through fear. Such was not Paul’s Christ, nor can that of any true apostle
“Celui de tous vrais et fideles ministres;” — “That of all true and faithful ministers.”
be such. Those, accordingly, have no ground to boast that they are ministers of Christ, who paint him in various colors with a view to their own advantage. For he alone is the true Christ, in whom there appears that uniform and unvarying yea, which Paul declares to be characteristic of him.
entries.6f9ef3ca596eb138eaaa97eba8f14e6c9169fe22:
20. For all the promises of God — Here again he shows how firm and unvarying the preaching of Christ ought to be, inasmuch as he is the groundwork
“Le fondement et la fermete;” — “The foundation and security.”
of all the promises of God. For it were worse than absurd to entertain the idea that he, in whom all the promises of God are established, is like one that wavers.
“Que celuy en qui toutes les promesses de Dieu sont establies et ratifices, fust comme vn homme chancelant et inconstant;” — “That he, in whom all the promises of God are established and ratified, should be like a man that is wavering and unsteady.”
Now though the statement is general, as we shall see ere long, it is, notwithstanding, accommodated to the circumstances of the case in hand, with the view of confirming the certainty of Paul’s doctrine. For it is not simply of the gospel in general that he treats, but he honors more especially his own gospel with this distinction. “If the promises of God are sure and well-founded, my preaching also must of necessity be sure, inasmuch as it contains nothing but Christ, in whom they are all established.” As, however, in these words he means simply that he preached a gospel that was genuine, and not adulterated by any foreign additions,
“Il a presché le vray et pur Evangile, et sans y auoir lien adiousté qu’il ait corrompu ou falsifié;” — “He preached the true and pure gospel, and without having added to it anything that had corrupted or adulterated it.”
let us keep in view this general doctrine, that all the promises of God rest upon Christ alone as their support — a sentiment that is worthy of being kept in remembrance, and is one of the main articles of our faith. It depends, however, on another principle — that it is only in Christ that God the Father is propitious to us. Now the promises are testimonies of his fatherly kindness towards us. Hence it follows, that it is in him alone that they are fulfilled.
The promises, I say, are testimonies of Divine grace: for although God shows kindness even to the unworthy, (Luke 6:35,) yet when promises are given in addition to his acts of kindness, there is a special reason — that in them he declares himself to be a Father. Secondly, we are not qualified for enjoying the promises of God, unless we have received the remission of our sins, which we obtain through Christ. Thirdly, the promise, by which God adopts us to himself as his sons, holds the first place among them all. Now the cause and root of adoption is Christ; because God is not a Father to any that are not members and brethren of his only-begotten Son. Everything, however, flows out from this source — that, while we are without Christ, we are hated by God rather than favorably regarded, while at the same time God promises us everything that he does promise, because he loves us. Hence it is not to be wondered if Paul here teaches, that all the promises of God are ratified and confirmed in Christ.
It is asked, however, whether they were feeble or powerless, previously to Christ’s advent; for Paul seems to speak here of Christ as manifested in the flesh. (1 Timothy 3:16.) I answer, that all the promises that were given to believers from the beginning of the world were founded upon Christ. Hence Moses and the Prophets, in every instance in which they treat of reconciliation with God, of the hope of salvation, or of any other favor, make mention of him, and discourse at the same time respecting his coming and his kingdom. I say again, that the promises under the Old Testament were fulfilled to the pious, in so far as was advantageous for their welfare; and yet it is not less true, that they were in a manner suspended until the advent of Christ, through whom they obtained their true accomplishment. And in truth, believers themselves rested upon the promises in such a way, as at the same time to refer the true accomplishment of them to the appearing of the Mediator, and suspended their hope until that time. In fine, if any one considers what is the fruit of Christ’s death and resurrection, he will easily gather from this, in what respect the promises of God have been sealed and ratified in him, which would otherwise have had no sure accomplishment.
Wherefore, also, through him let there be Amen. Here also the Greek manuscripts do not agree, for some of them have it in one continued statement — As many promises of God as there are, are in him Yea, and in him Amen to the glory of God through us.
“The most ancient MSS. and versions read the verse thus: — ὃσαι γὰρ ἐπαγγελίαι Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ναὶ διό καὶ δι ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ᾿Αμὴν, τῷ Θεῷ πρὸς” δοξαν δι ᾿ ἡμῶν;” — “For all the promises of God are in him yea; because they are, through him, who is the Amen, to the glory of God by us.” — Penn
The different reading, however, which I have followed, is easier, and contains a fuller meaning. For as he had said, that, in Christ, God has confirmed the truth of all his promises, so now he teaches us, that it is our duty to acquiesce in this ratification. This we do, when, resting upon Christ by a sure faith, we subscribe and set our seal that God is true, as we read in John 3:33, and that with a view to his glory, as this is the end to which everything should be referred. (Ephesians 1:13, and Romans 3:4.)
The other reading, I confess, is the more common one, but as it is somewhat meagre, I have not hesitated to prefer the one that contains the fuller meaning, and, besides, is much better suited to the context. For Paul reminds the Corinthians of their duty — to utter their Amen in return, after having been instructed in the simple truth of God. If, however, any one is reluctant to depart from the other reading, there must, in any case, be an exhortation deduced from it
“Qu’il scache tousiours qu’il en faut tirer vne exhortation;” — “Let him always know this — that we must deduce from it an exhortation.”
to a mutual agreement in doctrine and faith.
2 Corinthians 1:21-22
21. Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God;
21. Qui autem confirmat nos vobiscum in Christo, et qui unxit nos, Deus est:
22. Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.
22. Qui et obsignavit nos, et dedit arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris.
entries.7d2facb0425a73c90dad175210d44502c652d2d2:
God, indeed, is always true and steadfast in his promises, and has always his Amen, as often as he speaks. But as for us, such is our vanity, that we do not utter our Amen in return, except when he gives a sure testimony in our hearts by his word. This he does by his Spirit. That is what Paul means here. He had previously taught, that this is a befitting harmony — when, on the one hand, the calling of God is without repentance, (Romans 11:29,) and we, in our turn, with an unwavering faith, accept of the blessing of adoption that is held out to us. That God remains steadfast to his promise is not surprising; but to keep pace with God in the steadfastness of our faith in return — that truly is not in man’s power.
“D’apporter de nostre costé vne correspondance mutuelle à la vocation de Dieu en perseuerant constamment en la foy;” — “To maintain on our part a mutual correspondence to the call of God by persevering steadfastly in the faith.”
He teaches us, also, that God cures our weakness or defect, (as they term it,) when, by correcting our belief, he confirms us by his Spirit. Thus it comes, that we glorify him by a firm steadfastness of faith. He associates himself, however, with the Corinthians, expressly for the purpose of conciliating their affections the better, with a view to the cultivation of unity.
“Expressement afin de les gaigner et attirer a vraye vnite;” — “Expressly for the purpose of gaining them over and drawing to a true unity.”
