21. Who hath anointed us. He employs different terms to express one and the same thing. For along with confirmation, he employs the terms anointing and sealing, or, by this twofold metaphor,
“Par les deux mots qui sont dits par metaphore et similitude;” — “By these two words which are employed by way of metaphor and similitude.”
he explains more distinctly what he had previously stated without a figure. For God, by pouring down upon us the heavenly grace of the Spirit, does, in this manner, seal upon our hearts the certainty of his own word. He then introduces a fourth idea — that the Spirit has been given to us as an earnest — a similitude which he frequently makes use of, and is also exceedingly appropriate.
“Αῤρ᾿αβὡν and the Latin arrhabo are derived from the Hebrew ערבון (gnarabon) — a pledge or earnest; i.e., a part of any price agreed on, and paid down to ratify the engagement; German, Hand — gift.” — Bloomfield. “The word appears to have passed, probably as a commercial term, out of the Hebrew or Phenician into the western languages.” — Gesenius. — Ed.
For as the Spirit, in bearing witness of our adoption, is our security, and, by confirming the faith of the promises, is the seal (σφραγὶς), so it is on good grounds that he is called an earnest,
“If God having once given this earnest, should not also give the rest of the inheritance, he should undergoe the losse of his earnest, as Chrysostome most elegantly and soundly argueth.” — Leigh’s Annotations. — Ed.
because it is owing to him, that the covenant of God is ratified on both sides, which would, but for this, have hung in suspense.
“A seal was used for different purposes: to mark a person’s property, to secure his treasures, or to authenticate a deed. In the first sense, the Spirit distinguishes believers as the peculiar people of God; in the second, he guards them as his precious jewels; in the third, he confirms or ratifies their title to salvation. [...] An earnest is a part given as a security for the future possession of the whole. The Holy Ghost is the earnest of the heavenly inheritance, because he begins that holiness in the soul which will be perfected in heaven, and imparts those joys which are foretastes of its blessedness.” — Dick’s Theology, volume 3 — Ed.
Here we must notice, in the first place, the relation
“La correspondance mutuelle;” — “The mutual correspondence.”
which Paul requires between the gospel of God and our faith; for as every thing that God says is more than merely certain, so he wishes that this should be established in our minds by a firm and sure assent. Secondly, we must observe that, as an assurance of this nature is a thing that is above the capacity of the human mind, it is the part of the Holy Spirit to confirm within us what God promises in his word. Hence it is that he has those titles of distinction — the Anointing, the Earnest, the Comforter, and the Seal. In the third place we must observe, that all that have not the Holy Spirit as a witness, so as to return their Amen to God, when calling them to an assured hope of salvation, do on false grounds assume the name of Christians.
2 Corinthians 1:23-24
23. Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth.
23. Ego autem testem invoco Deum in animam meam, quod parcens vobis nondum venerim Corinthum.
24. Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand.
24. Non quod dominemur fidei vestrae, sed adiutores sumus
“Nous sommes adiuteurs de vostre ioye; ou, nous aidons a;” — “We are helpers of your joy, or, we aid.”
gaudii vestri: fide enim statis.
2 Corinthians 2:1-2
1. But I determined this with myself, that I would not come again to you in heaviness.
1. Decreveram autem hoc in me ipso, non amplius venire in tristitia ad vos.
“De ne venir à vous derechef auec tristesse, ou, pour vous apporter fascherie;” — “Not to come again to you in sorrow, or, to cause you distress.”
2. For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?
2. Si enim ego contristo vos: et quis est qui me exhilaret, nisi is qui erit tristitia affectus ex me?
entries.4d56badc3e7616d5f82a4c0a0a56dfcd638e96b3: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.23" sID="gen120982" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> <hi type="italic">I call God for a witness.</hi> He now begins to assign a reason for his change of purpose; for hitherto he has merely repelled calumny. When, however, he says that <hi type="italic">he spared them, </hi>he indirectly throws back the blame upon them, and thus shows them that it would be unfair if he were put to grief through their fault, but that it would be much more unfair if they should permit this; but most of all unfair if they should give their assent to so base a calumny, as in that case they would be substituting in their place an innocent person, as if he had been guilty of their sin. Now he <hi type="italic">spared </hi>them in this respect, that if he had come he would have been constrained to reprove them more severely, while he wished rather that they should of their own accord repent previously to his arrival, that there might be no occasion for a harsher remedy, <note n="303"> <div sID="gen120984" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Remede plus aspre et rigoureux</foreign>;” — “A harsher and more rigorous remedy.”<div eID="gen120984" type="x-p"/> </note> which is a signal evidence of more than paternal lenity. For how much forbearance there was in shunning this necessity, when he had just ground of provocation!<div eID="gen120983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120985" type="x-p"/>He makes use, also, of an oath, that he may not seem to have contrived something to serve a particular purpose. For the matter in itself was of no small importance, and it was of great consequence that he should be entirely free from all suspicion of falsehood and pretence. Now there are two things that make an oath lawful and pious — the occasion and the disposition. The <hi type="italic">occasion </hi>I refer to is, where an oath is not employed rashly, that is, in mere trifles, or even in matters of small importance, but only where there is a call for it. The <hi type="italic">disposition </hi>I refer to is, where there is not so much regard had to private advantage, as concern felt for the glory of God, and the advantage of the brethren: For this end must always be kept in view, that our oaths may promote the honor of God, and promote also the advantage of our neighbours in a matter that is befitting. <note n="304"> <div sID="gen120986" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Moyennant que ce soit en chose iuste et raisonable</foreign>;” — “Provided it is in a matter that is just and reasonable.”<div eID="gen120986" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120987" type="x-p"/>The form of the oath must also be observed — <hi type="italic">first, </hi>that he calls God to witness; and, <hi type="italic">secondly, </hi>that he says <hi type="italic">upon my soul</hi> For in matters that are doubtful and obscure, where man’s knowledge fails, we have recourse to God, that he, who alone is truth, may bear testimony to the truth. But the man that appeals to God as his witness, calls upon him at the same time to be an avenger of perjury, in the event of his declaring what is false. This is what is meant by the phrase <hi type="italic">upon my soul. </hi>“I do not object to his inflicting punishment upon me, if I am guilty of falsehood.” Although, however, this is not always expressed in so many words, it is, notwithstanding, to be understood. For<div eID="gen120987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120988" type="x-p"/>if we are unfaithful, God remaineth faithful<lb/> and will not deny himself (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Tim.2.13">2 Timothy 2:13</reference>.)<div eID="gen120988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120989" type="x-p"/>He will not suffer, therefore, the profanation of his name to go unpunished.<div eID="gen120989" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120982" osisID="2Cor.1.23" type="section"/>
entries.b4aec3b04a2d627c4c3755ee01c5b5181257d75f: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.1.24" sID="gen120990" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">Not that we exercise dominion</hi> He anticipates an objection that might be brought forward. “What! Do you then act so tyrannically <note n="305"> <div sID="gen120992" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Es — tu si insupportable, et si orgueilleux</foreign>?” — “Are you so insufferable and so proud?”<div eID="gen120992" type="x-p"/> </note> as to be formidable in your very look? Such were not the gravity of a Christian pastor, but the cruelty of a savage tyrant.” He answers this objection first <hi type="italic">indirectly, </hi>by declaring that matters are not so; and afterwards <hi type="italic">directly, </hi>by showing that the very circumstance, that he had been constrained to treat them more harshly, was owing to his fatherly affection. When he says that he does not <hi type="italic">exercise dominion over their faith, </hi>he intimates, that such a power is unjust and intolerable — nay more, is tyranny in the Church. For faith ought to be altogether exempt, and to the utmost extent free, from the yoke of men. We must, however, observe, who it is that speaks, for if ever there was a single individual of mortals, that had authority to claim for himself such a <hi type="italic">dominion, </hi>Paul assuredly was worthy of such a privilege. Yet he acknowledges, <note n="306"> <div sID="gen120993" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il confesse franchement</foreign>;” — “He frankly confesses.”<div eID="gen120993" type="x-p"/> </note> that it does not belong to him. Hence we infer, that faith owns no subjection except to the word of God, and that it is not at all in subjection to human control. <note n="307"> <div sID="gen120994" type="x-p"/> The views here expressed by Calvin are severely animadverted upon in the following terms by the Romanists, in the Annotations appended to the Rheims version of the New Testament: “Calvin and his seditious sectaries with other like which <hi type="italic">despise dominion</hi>, as St. Jude describeth such, would by this place deliver themselves from all yoke of spiritual Magistrates and Rulers: namely, that they be subject to no man touching their faith, or for the examination and trial of their doctrine, but to God and his word only. And no marvel that the malefactors and rebels of the Church would come to no tribunal but God’s, that so they may remain unpunished at least during this life. For though the Scriptures plainely condemne their heresies, yet they could writhe themselves out by false glosses, constructions, corruptions, and denials of the bookes to be canonical, if there were no lawes or judicial sentences of men to rule and represse them.” To these statements Dr. Fulke in his elaborate work in refutation of the errors of Popery, (Lond. 1601,) p. 559, appropriately replies as follows: “This is nothing els but a lewd and senselesse slander of Calvin and vs, that we despise lordship, because we will not be subject to the tyranny of Antichrist, that would be Lord of our faith, and arrogateth vnto himselfe auctoritie to make new articles of fayth, which have no ground or warrant in the word of God. But CALVIN did willingly acknowledge all auctoritie of the ministers of the Church, which the Scripture doth allow unto them, and both practiced, and submitted himselfe to the discipline of the Church, and the lawful gouernours thereof, although he would not yield unto the tyrannicall yoke of the Pope, who is neither soueraigne of the Church, nor any true member of the same. Yea, Calvin and we submit ourselves, not only to the auctoritie of the Church, but also of the Ciuile Magistrates to be punished, if we shall be found to teach or doe any thing contrary to the doctrine of faith, receyued and approved by the Church, whereas the Popish clergy, in causes of religion, will not be subject to the temporal gouernors, judgement, and correction.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120994" type="x-p"/> </note> Erasmus has observed in his Annotations, that by supplying the Greek particle <foreign xml:lang="el">ἕνεκα</foreign>, it may be understood in this way — <hi type="italic">Not that we exercise dominion over you</hi> — <hi type="italic">with respect to your faith</hi> — <hi type="italic">a </hi>rendering which amounts almost to the same thing. For he intimates, that there is no spiritual dominion, except that of God only. This always remains a settled point — pastors have no peculiar <hi type="italic">dominion </hi>over men’s consciences, <note n="308"> <div sID="gen120995" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que les Pasteurs et Evesques n’ont point de iurisdiction propre sur les consciences</foreign>;” — “That Pastors and Bishops have no peculiar jurisdiction over consciences.”<div eID="gen120995" type="x-p"/> </note> inasmuch as they are ministers, <hi type="italic">not lords. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.3">1 Peter 5:3</reference>.)<div eID="gen120991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120996" type="x-p"/>What then does he leave to himself and others? He calls them<hi type="italic"> helpers of their joy</hi> — by which term I understand <hi type="italic">happiness. </hi>At the same time he employs the term <hi type="italic">joy </hi>as opposed to the terror which tyrants awaken through means of their cruelty, and also false prophets, <note n="309"> <div sID="gen120997" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et les faux — apostres aussi</foreign>;” — “And false Apostles also.”<div eID="gen120997" type="x-p"/> </note> resembling tyrants, that <hi type="italic">rule with rigor and authority, </hi>as we read in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.34.4">Ezekiel 34:4</reference>. He argues from contraries, that he did by no means usurp dominion over the Corinthians, inasmuch as he endeavored rather to maintain them in the possession of a peace that was free, and full of joy.<div eID="gen120996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120998" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For by faith ye stand.</hi> As to the reason why he adds this, others either pass it over altogether in silence, or they do not explain it with sufficient distinctness. For my part, I am of opinion that he here again argues from contraries. For if the nature and effect of faith be such that we lean, in order that we may <hi type="italic">stand</hi>, <note n="310"> <div sID="gen120999" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Afin que nous demeurions fermes</foreign>;” — “In order that we may remain secure.”<div eID="gen120999" type="x-p"/> </note> it is absurd to speak of faith as being subject to men. Thus he removes that unjust dominion, with which, he had a little before declared, he was not chargeable.<div eID="gen120998" type="x-p"/><div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.1.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120990" osisID="2Cor.1.24" type="section"/><div eID="gen120968"/><div eID="gen120732"/> <div sID="gen121000"/> <div sID="gen121001" type="x-p"/>CHAPTER 2<div eID="gen121001" type="x-p"/>

               <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 PAul<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Will of God here doth not signifie the bare permission, but the Calling and Precept of God; he was called to be an A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.1. 1 <ns0:hi>Epist.</ns0:hi> 1.1. making him a <ns0:hi>Minister</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>Witness, Acts</ns0:hi> 26.16.</ns0:note>, and Timothy <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> brother, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the church of God, which is at Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rinth, with all the Saints which are in all Achaia <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">His joyning of <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> with him, shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth both the great humility of the Apostle, and his desire to give him a reputation in the Churches, though he was a very young man. The Epistle is not directed only to the Church of God, which was at <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> (the <ns0:hi>Metropolis</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Peloponnesus</ns0:hi>) but also to all those Christians which lived in <ns0:hi>Achaia:</ns0:hi> by which name probably he doth not understand all <ns0:hi>Graecia,</ns0:hi> though that anciently had that name from one <ns0:hi>Achaeus</ns0:hi> that was King there, from whom the Grecians had the name of <ns0:hi>Achivi</ns0:hi>) but that Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gion of <ns0:hi>Peloponnesus,</ns0:hi> which lay in a neck of Land between the <ns0:hi>Aegean</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ionian</ns0:hi> Sea, which obtained that name in a more special and restrained sense.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 1.3.</ns0:note> Grace <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> to you and peace from God our Father, and <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> the Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This was the Apostles common Salutation, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.7. See the Notes on the former Epistle, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.3. where it is ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servable, That not the Father only, but the Lord Jesus Christ, is invoked, and made the Author of Grace (which is the free Love of God) and of <ns0:hi>Pe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ce,</ns0:hi> which signifieth either reconcilia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion with God upon the free pardon of our sin, or union with men, and brotherly love amongst themselves. The Heathens used to begin their Epistles with wishing one another health and prosperity; but the Apostle hath shewn us a more Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian way, and more suited to the Faith of Christians, who be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve the Love and Favour of God, the greatest and most desi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable blessings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 1.3. 1 Pet. 1.3.</ns0:note> Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comforts <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It is an usual Form of Thanksgiving, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.25. & 9.5. It is in use with us, signifying our sincere and hearty desire that both we our selves might be inabled, and others by our Exam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples, might be quickened to speak well of God, and to praise his Name. This God is called the <ns0:hi>Father of our Lord Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi> that is, by <ns0:hi>Eternal Generation:</ns0:hi> He is also called the <ns0:hi>Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther of Mercies,</ns0:hi> because he is the Fountain of all that good which floweth to poor Creatures. And upon the same account he is also called the <ns0:hi>God of all-Comforts.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Who comforteth us in all our tribulation <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Vs,</ns0:hi> who are the Ministers of the Gospel, (as it may ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pear by what followeth) for the Apostle saith, That God doth it, that Ministers might, from the comforts wherewith God had comforted them, be able to comfort his people when they are under any trouble, either of body or mind, by the same Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thods and Arguments, which the holy Spirit had used and brought to their minds under trouble to relieve any of them. Two things are observable from this verse: 1. That the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle attributeth all the support, relief, and comfort, which he had under any tribulation, to God, as the Fountain and Author of all Mercy; for though possibly our comforts may be caused from the application of some promises in holy Writ, either cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led to our minds by the act of our own minds, or brought to our remembrance by some others, yet it is God who must make those Plaisters to stick, and to become healing and sanative to our Souls: So that he is the principal efficient Cause, though the Scriptures, or men, may be instrumental Causes. 2. That the Gifts, Graces, and Mercies that God bestoweth upon his Ministers, are bestowed upon them, not meerly for their own use, but for the use and good of others; to inable them to be serviceable in doing good to others Souls.</ns0:note>, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we our selves are comforted of God <ns0:hi>f.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:459" />5 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. 4.10.</ns0:note> as the sufferings of Christ abound in us <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He calleth his, and the other Apostles sufferings, the <ns0:hi>Suffer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings of Christ,</ns0:hi> either because they were sufferings for Christ; that is, for doing the work which Christ had given them to do: Or his and their personal sufferings as Members of that Body, of which Christ is the Head. Christ calleth <ns0:hi>Sauls</ns0:hi> persecuting the Saints, a persecuting of himself, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.4. Thus we read of <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> filling up that <ns0:hi>which is behind of the Sufferings of Christ, Col.</ns0:hi> 1.24.</ns0:note>, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">But, saith the Apostle, <ns0:hi>blessed be God,</ns0:hi> as we have many sufferings for Christ, so also we have many consolations by Christ. Christ, as God, is the efficient Cause of the Saints consolation; as Mediator, dying for us, he is the meritorious Cause; and it is by his Spirit (who is called the Comforter) that they are applied to us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And whether we be afflicted, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. 4.15.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> for your consolation and salvation <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Our sufferings tend to <ns0:hi>your Consolation</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Salvation,</ns0:hi> your Souls being upheld and supported by the sight of our boldness, and courage, and confidence in our sufferings: Thus <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 1.13, 14. <ns0:hi>My bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other places. And many of the brethren in the Lord waxing confi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.</ns0:hi> And his sufferings also were for their <ns0:hi>Salvation,</ns0:hi> as they encouraged them to suffer also; and, <ns0:hi>If we suffer with him, we shall reign with him, and our light and moment any afflictions shall work for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory</ns0:hi>:</ns0:note>, which is <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 paragraph">
                        <ns0:desc>〈1 paragraph〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">And (saith the Apostle) our suffering hath had a good ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect amongst you, while you, with Faith and patience, endure sufferings of the same sort which we endure and suffer.</ns0:note>: or whether we be comforted, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> for your consolation and salvation <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And if we be supported, upheld, and comforted under our suffer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings, the advantage of this also redoundeth to you, as you are incouraged to suffer for the Gospel and profession of Christ, from seeing how God supporteth us under our sufferings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And our hope of you <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> stedfast <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">We have a stedfast hope of you, that as you have endu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red sufferings for Christ and his Gospel, so you will still endure them, as we have done.</ns0:note>, knowing that as you are partakers of the sufferings, so <ns0:hi>shall ye be</ns0:hi> also of the consolation <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">And, we know, that as you are partakers of the Sufferings of Christ and his Gospel, so you shall also share in those Divine consolations that those feel who endure such sufferings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 For we would not, brethren, have you igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rant of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>5.32.</ns0:note> our trouble which came to us in Asia <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">We are at a great loss to determine what these troubles were in <ns0:hi>Asia,</ns0:hi> of which the Apostle doth here speak. We read of several troubles <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> met with in <ns0:hi>Asia</ns0:hi>; it was there he was in danger through the tumult raised by <ns0:hi>Demetrius, Acts</ns0:hi> 19.23. It was there (at <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi>) where <ns0:hi>he fought with beasts after the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of men</ns0:hi> (as he told us in the former Epistle.) Whoso readeth <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 19, & 20. of the <ns0:hi>Acts,</ns0:hi> will find the largest ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count we have in Scripture of the troubles <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> met with in <ns0:hi>Asia.</ns0:hi> But this Epistle is thought to have been written at a time, that will not agree to the time of those troubles; there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore they are thought to have been some troubles, of which we have a mention no where else in holy Writ.</ns0:note>, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Whatsoever they were, this Text tells us they were very great, and above his natural strength to have born; some think, above the strength of ordinary Christians, insomuch that if the Apostle had not found the more than ordinary assistances of the Spirit of God, he could not have stood under them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 But we had the <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>swer.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sentence of death in our selves <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">We verily thought we should have been killed, (and so it is expounded by the last words of the former verse) <ns0:hi>we despair<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed even of life.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, that we should <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 17.5, 7.</ns0:note> not trust in our selves, but in God, which raiseth the dead <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And this God did to teach us, That we should, when we are in dangers, look above the creature, and have no confidence in created means, but only look up to him, who raiseth from the dead. As <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> offered up <ns0:hi>Isaac, Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.17, 18, 19. <ns0:hi>Accounting that God <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> able to raise him from the dead. Abraham</ns0:hi> had a promise to bottom such a Faith upon; God had told him, That in <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> his seed should be called: So had <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> God having revealed to him, that he had a further work for him to do. So have not all Christians, we do not know our courses, nor what work God hath in his Eternal Counsels laid out for us; and therefore cannot be confident of deliverances in this life by the Almighty Power of God; but yet we, under our greatest tryals, may trust in God, who will certainly raise us from the dead; (of which Faith we have an instance in <ns0:hi>Iob, Chap.</ns0:hi> 19.25, 26, 27.) However for our comfort in our distres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses we may observe, That God, in his great deliverances of his people, useth to suffer them first to be brought to the greatest extremities; that <ns0:hi>in the Mount of the Lord</ns0:hi> it may be seen, and that they may learn to know that their Salvations are from him; more from his Almighty Power, than from the virtue of any means they can use, (though yet it be our duty to use what lawful means his Providence affordeth us.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Who delivered us from so great a death <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>So great a death,</ns0:hi> in this Text signifies no more than so great a tryal of affliction; as he elsewhere saith, he was <ns0:hi>in deaths often,</ns0:hi> that is, in dangers of death.</ns0:note>, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver <ns0:hi>us</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Nor (saith the Apostle) were we only at that time in danger of our lives, nor had we only, at that time, an experience of Gods Power, Good<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, and Faithfulness in our deliverance; but we are in jeopar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy every hour, and experience the Power of God in our deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verance yet every day. And it being for the advantage of the Church of Christ, that our lives should be prolonged, (though we desire rather to be dissolved, and to be with Christ) we are confident that he will yet deliver. Former experiences of Gods goodness in delivering us out of troubles, ought to increase our Faith, and beget a confidence in us, that God will de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liver us, (if it may be for his own Glory, and our good.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 You also <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.30. Phil. 1.19. Philem. 22.</ns0:note> helping together by prayer for us <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Faith ought not to hinder Prayer; nor doth Gods princi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pal Efficiency, as to any Mercy or Deliverance bestowed upon us, give a <ns0:hi>Supersede<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s</ns0:hi> to us, as to the use of any means, whether Natural or Spiritual, by which the Mercy may be obtained. Nor are the Prayers of the meanest Saints useless for the great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est, or beneath their desires; men and womens favour with God depends not upon their order, station, and repute in the World.</ns0:note>, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.15.</ns0:note> for the gift <ns0:hi>bestowed</ns0:hi> upon us by the means of many persons, thanks may be given by many on our behalf <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">By the Gift here, he means the deliverance before mentioned; which he calls a <ns0:hi>Gift,</ns0:hi> to denote, not only Gods principal Efficiency in it, but his free bestowing of it; this Gift (he saith) is bestowed by the means of many, because obtained upon the Intercession or Prayers of many. God doth therefore bestow mercies upon particular persons at the inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cession of many others on their behalf, that he may not only have the praises of those persons upon whom he so bestoweth the mercy; but of those who have been so praying. The Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle hereby hinteth to us, That we ought no more to forget to give thanks for others, for whom God hath heard us, than to pray for them when in distress.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For our rejoycing is this, the testimony of our consciences, that in simplicity and godly since<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He declareth the confidence that he had, that he should not want their Prayers, because his own heart told him, to his joy and satisfaction, that however others might reproach him, as if he had carried himself deceitfully, or craftily; yet he had not done so, but had lived in the World in all <ns0:hi>simplicity</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>sincerity</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> (so the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> is.) Simplicity is opposed to <ns0:hi>double-mindedness</ns0:hi>; where there is a composition in a man, a mixture of truth and falshood, fairness in speech, and falshood in heart or action. Sincerity is opposed to <ns0:hi>Hypocrisie.</ns0:hi> It is said to be <ns0:hi>of God,</ns0:hi> because he is the God of Truth, hath com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded it, approveth it, worketh it, and disposeth the heart of man to it.</ns0:note>, not with fleshly wisdom <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This is opposed to <ns0:hi>fleshly Wisdom,</ns0:hi> which prompteth a man to seek his own ends any way, good or bad.</ns0:note>, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">But (saith the Apostle) we have had our conversation in the World, not by the guidance of any such corrupt habit or Principle, but by the <ns0:hi>Grace of God,</ns0:hi> the love and fear of God dwelling in us; or, we have done this, not of our selves, but, by the guidance and assistance of Divine Grace, helping us so, to live, and to have our conversation in the World.</ns0:note>, and more abundantly to you-wards <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And more especially you are our Witnesses of this, amongst whom we have preached the Gospel freely, so as we have not made it chargeable to you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For we write no other things unto you, then what you read, or acknowledge, and I trust you shall acknowledge even to the end <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I do not tell you stories, the things which I write, and which you read, either in my Epistles to you, or to other Churches of Christ, are what you know must owne and ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledge to be truth; and I hope you shall acknowledge them to be so to the end both of my life and yours.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:460" />14 As also you have acknowledged us in part, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5.12.</ns0:note> we are your rejoicing, even as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 2.16. & 4.1. 1 Thess. 2.19, 20.</ns0:note> ye also <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> ours in the day of the Lord Jesus <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>In part,</ns0:hi> may either refer to persons, or things; part of you have so owned and acknowledged us, though others of you have abused us. Or you have <ns0:hi>in part,</ns0:hi> or at <ns0:hi>some times,</ns0:hi> owned us, that you had cause to bless God for us, and to rejoyce, that God ever sent us to preach the Gospel amongst you. And as some have owned us as their joy, or all of you have at some times acknowledged us as such; so you are also <ns0:hi>our rejoycing</ns0:hi>; we rejoyce that God hath made our labour suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessful to your Souls, and I trust in the day when the Lord Jesus shall come to judge the World, you shall be more our rejoycing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And in this confidence I was minded to come to you before, that you might have a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.11.</ns0:note> second <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>grace.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> benefit <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Being confident that my presence with you, would be matter of rejoycing both to you, and also to me, I purpo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed to come unto you before I went into <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> visiting you shortly in my journey thither, that so you might have a second longer visit in kindness to you. We find, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 16.9. that <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> received his first Call into <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> in a Vision; we read again of his passing through <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> to go to <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem:</ns0:hi> The Apostle seemeth to speak here of the latter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And to pass by you into Macedonia, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 16.5.</ns0:note> to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judea <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He had purposed to take <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> in his way unto <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> and after he had finished his business in <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> his reso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lutions were to have come back to <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> and to stay with them some time; hoping to have some of their company some part of the way toward <ns0:hi>Iudea:</ns0:hi> But it seems, though he thus purposed, yet God had otherwise ordered his motions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Though the Apostle doth not in so many words tell us so, yet it is apparent from this verse, That some of the <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rinthians</ns0:hi> had taken occasion from his not coming at this time to <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> to charge him with <ns0:hi>levity</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>inconstancy</ns0:hi>; as if his words were not to be regarded. It is very observable, how little things the men of the World will take advantage from, to vilifie and lessen the reputation of Gods faithful Ministers and People. How many others might have promised to be in such a place at such a time, and have failed, without the reproach of the men in the World? Who would have been so charitable to them, as to have excused them, by saying, They spake according to their present intentions and resolutions; but they were hindred by the Providence of God: but if <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> fails, they will interpret it to be from the lightness and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />constancy of his mind. So charitable is the World to its own, so uncharitable to those who are not of the World, but by God called out of the World. From this imputation the Apostle cleareth himself, denying that he used <ns0:hi>lightness,</ns0:hi> and that his not coming proceeded from any levity or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> inconstancy of mind; for he fully did purpose to have come.</ns0:note>? Or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or did (faith he) I purpose after the manner of carnal men, who make no conscience of their word? who promise and deny both in a breath?</ns0:note>, that with me there should be Yea, yea, and Nay, nay? <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Should there be in me such a Spirit, as to speak a thing with my lips which my heart doth not agree to? This lets us know, that <ns0:hi>Truth</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Steadiness</ns0:hi> are things which do highly commend either a Minister, or a Christian; but especially him who is a Minister of the Gospel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 But <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> true, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>our prea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ching.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> our word toward you was not Yea, and Nay <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As God is true to his Promises, so he hath taught me to be true to mine. Some make these words not to be meerly declarative of the Truth of God, but a kind of an Oath, or cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling the God of Truth to witness, that his <ns0:hi>Word towards them</ns0:hi>; by which some understand the Gospel, or the Word which he had preached amongst them, (and of that indeed lie speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in the next verse) but to me it seemeth much less strain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, to interpret <ns0:hi>Pauls word</ns0:hi> in this verse of that word of pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise, of which he had before spoken; the promise which he owned before that he had made them of his coming to them. That <ns0:hi>word,</ns0:hi> he saith, was not <ns0:hi>yea, and nay,</ns0:hi> that is, he did not make it with a quite contrary intention; but when he promi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, he faithfully intended to have justified his word, and indeed to have come; but the Providence of God, to which all men are subjected, had otherwise ordered him and dispo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed of him; which was the cause why he had not yet been as good as his word. It is very observable, how careful this great Apostle was to clear himself from any imputatio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vity and falshood; and it should teach us to be careful to maintain our reputation in the world, for truth and steadiness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> by me, and Silva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nus, and Timotheus <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Apostle here giveth a reason, why he had made <ns0:hi>Truth</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sincerity</ns0:hi> so much his business (which reason obli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geth us also, who are as much bound as he, to study a con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formity to Christ) saith he, <ns0:hi>The Son of God who was preached among you,</ns0:hi> that is, Christ Jesus; (who, though (as some ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve) is in these Epistles no where called <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Lord</ns0:hi>) is here called the <ns0:hi>Son of God</ns0:hi>; which can be understood in no other sense, than by Eternal generation; for those who are only the Sons of God by <ns0:hi>Adoption,</ns0:hi> are not the subjects of Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisters preaching. We read of this <ns0:hi>Silvanus,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.1. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.21. Some think that he was the same person who is called <ns0:hi>Silas, Acts</ns0:hi> 16.19. Of <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> we have heard before. They were both Ministers, who (as well as <ns0:hi>Apollos</ns0:hi> before men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned) had laboured in the Gospel amongst the <ns0:hi>Corinthians.</ns0:hi> Now (saith the Apostle) that Christ whom both I, and other Ministers of the Gospel, have preached to you, is not incer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain and inconstant, one thing at one time, and in one place, another thing at another time, and in another place.</ns0:note>, was not Yea, and Nay, but in him was Yea <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He was only one and the same; his Doctrine was always certain and uniform, and consistent with it self; and our conversa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion ought to be suitable to him and his Doctrine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For all the promises of God in him <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> Yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">As Christ was <ns0:hi>yea,</ns0:hi> and all his Doctrine certain and uni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />form, so all the Promises of God are <ns0:hi>yea</ns0:hi>; the Promises of the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> have their <ns0:hi>yea</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Amen</ns0:hi> in him; all the Promises of Grace, whatsoever is promised to Believers, shall be veri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied by him, that so God may be glorified, and have from men the honour of being always esteemed a true and faithful God; one that cannot fail and falsifie his word. But how are the Promises of God <ns0:hi>yea</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Amen</ns0:hi> in Christ <ns0:hi>by us? Answ.</ns0:hi> As the Ministers of the Gospel are the Ministers of Christ for the explication and application of them. The Promises are from the Father, through Christ as the meritorious Cause, and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternally applied by the holy Spirit, while they are more ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternally applied by the Ministers of the Gospel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Anointing</ns0:hi> here mentioned, is doubtless the same men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned by S. <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2.20, 27. by which is understood the holy Spirit: so as Gods <ns0:hi>anointing</ns0:hi> his people signifies his gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving them his holy Spirit, to dwell and to work in them; which holy Spirit diffuseth it self throughout the whole Soul of the Believer, (as the <ns0:hi>Oyl</ns0:hi> of old poured out upon the he<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of the <ns0:hi>Kings, High-Priests,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Prophets.</ns0:hi>) Believers are <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to be <ns0:hi>anointed,</ns0:hi> because God hath by his Spirit, given to them, declared, That he hath set them apart to be <ns0:hi>Kings,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Priests,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Royal Priesthood.</ns0:hi> The same God also <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> their Souls both in Faith, and Love: and all in Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> him as our Head, and through him as the meritorious <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of all that Grace wherein we stand. It is observable, That how much soever vain man may ascribe to the power of mans Will, yet the blessed Apostle attributeth all to God; both our <ns0:hi>Anointing,</ns0:hi> the first infusion of gracious habits, and also our <ns0:hi>Establishing.</ns0:hi> It is Grace by which we stand.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Who <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 1.13. & 4.30.</ns0:note> hath also sealed us <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The use of a Seal is for confirmation of the thing to which it is affixed; the effect of it is the making the impression of it self upon the Wax: so as <ns0:hi>sealing</ns0:hi> us, both in this and other Texts, signifi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s both the confirmation of the Love of God to our Souls, and also the renewing and Sanctification of our Natures, imprinting the Image of God upon our Souls, ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king us (as the Apostle <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> saith) <ns0:hi>partakers of the Divin<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Nature;</ns0:hi> but the first seemeth probably to be most intended here.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 2.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> given us the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">We have the same expression <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 5.5. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.14. We read of the <ns0:hi>First-fruits of the Spirit, Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.23. The giving unto Believers the holy Spirit, and those saving spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual habits, which are his effects in the Soul, are both the <ns0:hi>First-fruits,</ns0:hi> and an <ns0:hi>Earnest</ns0:hi>; for as the <ns0:hi>First-fruits</ns0:hi> assured the Harvest, and the <ns0:hi>Earnest</ns0:hi> is a sure pledge of the bargain, when those who give it are honest and faithful; so the sanctifying habits, wrought in the Soul by the Spirit of Holiness, are a certain pledge of that Glory which shall be the portion of Believers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Moreover, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> I call God to record upon my soul, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 4.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Chap. 2.3.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 12.20. & <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2, 10.</ns0:note> to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Here is a perfect form of an <ns0:hi>Oath,</ns0:hi> which is nothing else but a <ns0:hi>solemn</ns0:hi> calling of God to witness the truth of what we speak, whether promising, or asserting. Those words, <ns0:hi>upon my Soul</ns0:hi> also, have the force of an <ns0:hi>imprecation,</ns0:hi> but it is in a very serious thing: the Apostle was deeply charged with <ns0:hi>lev<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>y,</ns0:hi> for not making good his promise in coming, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he reasonably presumed, that some amongst them would be difficult to believe the true cause; to gain credit with them, he takes a voluntary Oath, which in weighty matters is lawful, (though sometimes it be done not before a Magi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strate.) The thing he thus attests, is, That he hitherto had forborn to come out of kindness to them; to <ns0:hi>spare them</ns0:hi> (as he phraseth it) which may either be understood of their <ns0:hi>pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses,</ns0:hi> (for he could not have gone without some charge to them, though he took no standing Salary from them for preaching:) or (as others possibly judge better) <ns0:hi>to spare their persons</ns0:hi>; for it he had come before, they had reformed those abuses that were amongst them, he must (as he before spake) have come unto them <ns0:hi>with a rod.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:460" />24 Not for <ns0:note place="margin">1 Cor. 3.5. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 5.3.</ns0:note> that we have dominion over your faith <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not (say some) that we pretend or boast of any domi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nion over you, because of your Faith, as if upon that account we would be chargeable, and exact monies of you: But their Interpretation is better, who think that by these words the Apostle removes from himself, and much more from all in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feriour Ministers, any power of imposing upon people to be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve any thing, but what God had in his Word revealed as the object of Faith. He had in the verse before used the Phrase <ns0:hi>spare you,</ns0:hi> which he thought might sound harsh in their ears, and give some occasion to carp at him, as if he designed some Lordly power over them: No, (saith the Apostle) though I speak of sparing you, I intend no exercise of Lordly power,</ns0:note>, but are helpers of your joy <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">but only to promote your joy, by removing those things which hinder your true rejoycing. Your present glorying is not good, while these disorders, contrary to the Will of God, are amongst you; and you are full of contentions and divi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions, which hinder your comfortable society and communion together, as one Body.</ns0:note>

                     </ns0:gap> 11.20.</ns0:note> by faith ye stand <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The most of you <ns0:hi>stand in the Faith,</ns0:hi> (so some interpret the latter part of the verse.) I should rather make this the sense, <ns0:hi>By Faith you must stand</ns0:hi>; if you err in matters of Faith, (as some of this Church had done in the business of the Resurrection, as the Apostle told us in the 15. Chapter of the first Epistle) you fall; you no longer <ns0:hi>stand,</ns0:hi> than you keep the Faith pure and incorrupt. For, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of their Errors, as to the Resurrection, I cannot tell how to make the Apostles sense to be what some Learned men make it to bear, That he had nothing to blame in them in matters of <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> but only in some things referring to <ns0:hi>Order</ns0:hi>; and therefore <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>hey need not to suspect his exercise of any dominion over their Faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
